Net school spending excludes debt service, capital, transportation and food service — stated in the town’s own record, to the Finance Committee on 20 March 2024: “This is the minimum spending every school district must spend not including debt services, capital transportation, meals.” Because of those exclusions no figure in the town’s appropriation, the district’s budget book or the MUNIS ledger equals the net school spending DESE reports, and nothing in this archive maps the district’s line items onto DESE’s definition. So a reader cannot get from a budget line they can see to the one number the state enforces. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE, whose schedules derive net school spending from the district’s own accounts line by line; requestable from the Superintendent’s office or from DESE.

rows.what: What the student activity fee is for 2026-27, and what period the $70 covers
rows.why: The School Committee voted a universal student activity fee of $70, up from $55, on 7 May 2025 — the motion carried and the minute records the amount and no period. So whether a family pays $70 a child once a year, once a term, or once for each activity joined is not established, and those are a threefold difference on the same household. Nothing in this archive restates the fee for 2026-27 at all, and it is charged. — closes: the adopted student activity fee schedule for the 2026-27 school year, stating whether the fee is per student per year, per activity, or a base fee with activity fees on top, and any family cap or free/reduced provision.

rows.what: Whether the district charges anything for music, and what an instrument costs a family
rows.why: A resident told the School Committee on 26 February 2025 that "Instruments cost a lot, you need reeds and that can cost $50 a semester", and that band families "just aren’t paying anything directly to the school". That establishes music as a real household cost and establishes nothing about a district charge: no music fee, instrument rental rate or materials fee appears anywhere in this archive. A cost paid to a shop and a fee paid to the district are different things and neither is currently priced. — closes: the district’s music program fee schedule for 2026-27, or a statement that it charges no music fee and rents no instruments.

rows.what: What the processing fee is on every school payment made online
rows.why: The Superintendent’s email of 17 August 2026 tells families paying online that "RevTrak charges a small processing fee" and does not say what it is. It is added to every other fee a family pays through the portal, so it scales with the rest of the bill rather than sitting beside it, and a household paying athletics, bus and activity fees online pays it three times. "Small" is not a rate. — closes: the RevTrak merchant agreement or the portal’s own fee disclosure, stating whether the charge is a percentage, a flat amount per transaction, or both.

rows.what: What a family spends in the cafeteria when the standard meal is free
rows.why: Massachusetts funds universal free school meals and the district takes the programme, so the standard reimbursable meal is not billed to a household — that much is established and it is a real reduction in what families pay. What is outside the programme is not: a la carte items, snacks and second meals are charged, and no price list for them is held here. The School Lunch fund’s own revenue cannot separate the two. — closes: the district’s cafeteria a la carte price list for 2026-27.

rows.what: What a single-child family pays for the bus at the reduced rate in 2026-27
rows.why: The Superintendent’s May 2025 email states five bus tiers for FY2026 including $50 for a single-child family qualifying for a reduced fee. The August 2026 email for FY2027 states three tiers and does not restate that one. Whether the tier was dropped or simply omitted from the email is not established, and the difference decides whether a qualifying single-child household pays $50, $180, or nothing. — closes: the adopted transportation fee schedule for 2026-27, with every tier and the free/reduced provision, as approved by the School Committee.

rows.what: How much of a receiving district’s per-pupil spending Lunenburg actually pays
rows.why: 177 Lunenburg children were educated outside Lunenburg Public Schools in FY2026 and DESE publishes what each receiving district spends for every pupil, all funds. It does not publish what LUNENBURG pays towards any of it, and the two are different quantities by construction: a receiving district’s per-pupil figure is its whole spending over its whole pupil count, paid for by its own levy, its own Chapter 70 aid, its grants and its revolving funds as well as by any tuition or assessment. Lunenburg’s side arrives as three unlike mechanisms — a member-town assessment for Montachusett, a school choice tuition set by statute, and a charter tuition set by formula — and none of them equals the receiving district’s per-pupil figure. So the honest statement is that the districts our children go to spend more for each pupil than Lunenburg does; what a Lunenburg child costs the town at each of them cannot be read off it. — closes: the Town’s cherry sheet assessment detail for the fiscal year, which states the charter tuition, school choice tuition and regional assessment by receiving district, set beside DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for each of those districts.

rows.what: What Lunenburg receives for a child who chooses IN, and what the fall from 51 to 15 is worth
rows.why: DESE counts the children arriving in Lunenburg from other towns in every school year from SY2014 to SY2026: 51 at the start, 15 at the end, a fall of 71% while the number leaving stayed flat. The town’s own School Choice fund receipts fell over the ten years the two series share, from $220,058 in FY2014 to $116,976 in FY2023. Neither document states a RATE. The statutory base tuition is set by M.G.L. c.76 §12B, no document in this archive states it, and it is higher for special education; the arriving children also come by three different mechanisms — school choice, tuition waived by local agreement, and foster placement — which do not carry money the same way. So the two series can be published side by side and cannot be divided into each other: a per-student figure produced that way would be an assumption in a measurement’s clothes, and the money value of a 71% fall in arrivals is therefore not established anywhere on this site. — closes: the DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-ER (estimated receipts) for Lunenburg, which prints School Choice Receiving Tuition as its own receipt line, for the years the DESE counts cover.

rows.what: How many school choice seats Lunenburg opened, by grade and by year
rows.why: Children arriving from other towns fell from 51 in SY2014 to 15 in SY2026. Two readings fit that equally well and the published record separates them in one year only. A receiving district DECIDES each year how many school choice seats to open and at which grades — the School Committee minutes record that decision being taken on 22 January 2025 (elementary seats against high school only, tabled until the budget was settled), on 16 April 2025 (options beyond grade 9, moved contingent on free cash passing) and on 4 February 2026 (“We are looking to only add school choice options to the high school”). So fewer arrivals is consistent with fewer seats offered and equally consistent with fewer families applying. The Superintendent stated both counts to the Finance Committee on 26 February 2026 — 24 seats opened, 5 students applied — which points at applications for that one year and cannot speak for the other twelve. — closes: the School Committee’s annual school choice vote, seats by grade, for every year from SY2014 onward; the minutes hold it in pieces and nobody has compiled it as a series.

rows.what: What share of the schools’ grounds, custodial, heating and utility cost is athletics
rows.why: The town’s ledger codes every school account to a function, and athletics is function 3510 — 12 accounts, $518,334 appropriated in FY2026, which ties to the cent to the district’s own budget book. Custodians, heating, utilities, grounds and building maintenance are separate functions in the same printout, $2,035,523 revised across the whole school department in FY2026, and **not one of those accounts carries the athletics program segment**. The fields are mown, the gym is lit and heated and the lines are painted, so some of that $2,035,523 is a cost of school sports — but nothing published splits it out, no document states an allocation, and the athletics revolving fund’s cashbook does not name a field, a light or a custodian on any of its 277 postings. So every published athletics total, including this project’s, is a **floor and not a total**. — closes: a cost allocation from the district or the Town Accountant apportioning functions 4110, 4120, 4130, 4210 and 4220 across the programmes that use the buildings and grounds; failing that, the accounts-payable detail behind the grounds-maintenance warrants, which would at least name what was mown, lined or resurfaced and when.

rows.what: Whether a position the district announced it would cut was removed
rows.why: The district publishes a cut list most budget cycles — 158 named reductions across five cycles in this archive — and nothing published says what became of any of them. The only independent series that reaches any of it is DESE teacher FTE by school and subject, one October snapshot a year, and teachers are a minority of every list: paraprofessionals, secretaries, custodians, guidance staff, social workers, maintenance and BCBAs are counted by nothing at school level. **A list of intended cuts is not a record of staffing.** — closes: the district’s year-end position control report — filled posts by FTE, school and funding source — which the Business Office produces for payroll and does not publish.

rows.what: Whether an announced cut was reversed by a hire during the school year
rows.why: Residents describe posts being cut in the spring and filled again a month into the school year. The one instrument that reaches teacher staffing is DESE’s EPIMS return, collected on **1 October**, so a post cut in June and refilled in November is invisible to it and a post filled on 1 October and vacated in January counts as filled. Nothing in this archive is a within-year series. — closes: the district’s monthly payroll position report, or the School Committee’s personnel action items compiled as a series — the minutes carry appointments one meeting at a time and nobody has assembled them.

rows.what: What each announced school position cut was worth
rows.why: Only the FY2027 documents print a dollar figure beside a position. The FY2026 list the School Committee approved names 39 positions and prints no amount against any of them; the FY2025 impact slides print an FTE and a consequence and no money. So the register can say what was cut and, for one cycle in five, what it saved — and a figure beside a post is a budget-line saving, net of grants and fees (rule 11), rather than what the post costs. — closes: the personnel cost worksheet behind each year’s approved school budget, from the Business Office.

rows.what: How many Lunenburg children are educated at private or parochial schools
rows.why: DESE publishes where a town’s resident children go to school by receiving district, every year since SY2014 — and every row is keyed on the eight-digit code that identifies a Massachusetts PUBLIC district. Private schools do not have one and do not report enrolment to the state, so a Lunenburg child at Cushing Academy, Notre Dame or St Bernard’s generates no record: not a zero, not an “other”, nothing, for any town in any year (checked across the whole table). WHAT THIS BREAKS: the count of children educated outside Lunenburg’s own schools — 177 in FY2026 — is a FLOOR and reads as a total. A resident asked why Cushing was missing before the page admitted the limit. AND IT MATTERS IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM THE REST: a child at a private school costs the town no tuition and no assessment, and moves Chapter 70 aid by about $150 a pupil, so those departures are close to free for the school budget. They are the only kind of leaving that does not cost money, and they are the kind nobody can count. IT IS NOT: evidence that the number is large, or small. Nothing here bounds it at all. — closes: the town census, which counts every resident child of school age regardless of where they enrol, or the district’s own October 1 resident count, which is compiled annually and not published.

rows.what: How many paraprofessionals Lunenburg needs, against how many it employs
rows.why: 603 CMR 28.06(6)(d) is now in this archive, and it sets the class-size rule everybody argues around: a substantially separate group may not exceed eight students to one certified special educator, or twelve to a special educator AND AN AIDE. So a paraprofessional is partly what PERMITS a larger group rather than being a ratio in itself — which means paraprofessional counts track PROGRAM STRUCTURE and not student headcount, and would explain the thing /school-staffing measures and cannot account for: paras rising while enrolment fell. WHAT STILL CANNOT BE COMPUTED: the regulation binds INSTRUCTIONAL GROUPS and nothing published says how many groups Lunenburg runs, how large each is, or how its 41 substantially separate students are divided among them. 41 students could be four groups or seven, needing very different staffing, and both are lawful. THREE THINGS THAT WOULD DEFEAT ANY RATIO ANYWAY, all in the regulation itself: the sizes are MAXIMUMS and districts are expected to go smaller for complex needs (28.06(6)(c)); grouping must match each student’s own IEP, which can require one-to-one support no class-size rule predicts (b); and a group at maximum may take two further students mid-year by decision of the Administrator of Special Education (e). IT IS NOT: evidence that staffing is too high or too low. Nothing here supports either. — closes: the district’s own list of special education instructional groups by school and setting, with the students and staff assigned to each — compiled for DESE’s program approval under 603 CMR 28.09 and not published.

rows.what: Whether an “aide” in the class-size regulation is a paraprofessional the town budgets
rows.why: 603 CMR 28.06(6) sets every group size in terms of a certified special educator AND AN AIDE — a group of eight becomes lawful at twelve because an aide is present. 28.02(3) defines the certified special educator in full and the regulation defines no counterpart for the aide anywhere; the word “paraprofessional” appears in the whole of 603 CMR 28.00 only in the staff-training clauses of 28.03(1)(a), one of which names “teachers, paraprofessionals, and teacher assistants” as three separate things. DESE’s staffing return and every Lunenburg budget line say paraprofessional. So the term that DECIDES whether a group of twelve is lawful cannot be matched to any post the town funds, and a count of paraprofessionals is not a count of aides in the regulation’s sense. This sits directly under the gap about how many paraprofessionals the town needs: even with the group list, the units would not match. — closes: DESE’s guidance on what qualifies a person as an aide for 603 CMR 28.06(6), or the district’s own job descriptions mapped to that clause.

rows.what: Where 16 of Lunenburg’s students with disabilities are placed, in FY2026
rows.why: DESE’s placement breakdown prints four categories — Full Inclusion, Partial Inclusion, Substantially Separate and Separate School in District — and in FY2026 they sum to 242 of the 258 the same file prints as the total. Element DOE034 has nine acceptable values and this breakdown is in-district only, so the other 16 children are in categories the file does not print, and nothing published says which. That bounds every reading of the placement mix: the four printed rows are not a partition, and adding them and treating the result as the whole is the same error as summing a column that was never the total’s parts. — closes: DESE’s full DOE034 distribution for Lunenburg, or the district’s 1 October SIMS placement submission.

rows.what: What the special education staffing ratio requires moment to moment
rows.why: 603 CMR 28.06(6) sets the group sizes everybody quotes — eight students to one certified special educator, twelve with an aide — and residents are asking a further question the regulation does not answer: what happens when the group splits, when students go to recess or specials, or when the teacher leaves the room. THE FULL TEXT WAS SEARCHED. There is no mention of recess, none of "under the direction of", nothing about a group dividing, and nothing about a teacher stepping out. The only supervision clause is general and applies to every student in the Commonwealth: "The school staff shall at all times provide appropriate supervision of students while they are engaged in any school related activity on or off school grounds." And 28.06(6) says nothing about an aide beyond the two group-size clauses — it never defines what an aide does, what qualifications one needs, or whether one may supervise alone. WHAT THIS MEANS: the ratio governs THE SIZE OF AN INSTRUCTIONAL GROUP, not the staffing of a moment. It is not a supervision rule and cannot be read as one, in either direction — it neither permits nor forbids a paraprofessional holding a group while the teacher steps out. This is the second time this regulation has turned out to bind less than people assume. — closes: the district’s own program descriptions filed for DESE approval under 603 CMR 28.09, which describe staffing as operated rather than as capped; an individual IEP, which CAN specify one-to-one support at named times and is the only document that binds a moment; and the paraprofessional provisions of the collective bargaining agreement, for duties and coverage.

rows.what: Whether an aide assigned to one child also counts as the aide that raises a group from eight students to twelve
rows.why: 603 CMR 28.06(6)(c) and (d) raise the maximum group size from eight students to twelve when the certified special educator is "assisted by one aide". The regulation never defines the aide, never states their duties, and — searched on every build for eight phrasings — contains NO rule about one-to-one support of any kind. So where a child’s IEP assigns an aide to that child, nothing published says whether that person also satisfies the tier. THE DIRECTION OF THE ERROR IS THE POINT: assuming they do understates the staffing a group needs, and assuming they do not overstates it, so neither assumption is safe and this project makes neither. It is the same wall as the paraprofessional gap, hit from the other side — the rule counts students and the staffing record counts posts, and nothing converts one into the other. — closes: DESE’s program approval materials under 603 CMR 28.09, which describe how each approved group is staffed; or the district’s own group descriptions naming which adults are counted against which tier.

rows.what: Which courses a Lunenburg High student could actually choose from, in any year
rows.why: DESE publishes sections by SUBJECT AREA and never by course, so an elective ending is invisible inside a subject total that rose — a student told the School Committee on 7 February 2024 that Music Tech would be "non-existent", and the high school's Arts sections went from 24 that year to 25 the next. Both statements are true and this archive cannot hold them together. — closes: The district’s own Program of Studies for each year, which the High School Principal handed the School Committee on 6 March 2024, and the LHS master schedule presented to the School Committee on 4 December 2024. Neither is published.

rows.what: What is taught in the fifth of Lunenburg High sections DESE files as Miscellaneous
rows.why: 51 of the high school’s 247 sections in SY2025, averaging 4.9 students, in a subject area DESE gives no course names for — and the single largest mover in the section count since SY2017. The only public account of one is a student describing a new elective with four on the register and eight on the first day. — closes: The LHS master schedule by year, or the district’s own Student Course Schedule submission to DESE, which holds the course records the published aggregate is built from.

rows.what: How many classes ran in each subject at the two elementary schools
rows.why: The counts swing by a factor of two between adjacent years with no matching change in enrolment, and two school-years report an average class size no primary school can have — 87.1 at Lunenburg Primary in SY2011 and 36.5 in SY2022, against a maximum of 24.1 everywhere else. The subject coding of a self-contained classroom is not stable enough to trend, so the elementary half of the district cannot be read at all. — closes: DESE’s Student Course Schedule submission detail for Lunenburg, which carries the course records behind the published aggregate.

rows.what: Whether Lunenburg’s paraprofessionals moved out of special education, or were recoded, or the state changed what it counts
rows.why: Two DESE files count Lunenburg paraprofessionals over FY2020–FY2025 and move in opposite directions. The district comparison sheet’s all-programmes `Paraprofessional FTE` rises 57.0 to 67.0; the special education staff table in `n62c-bx65` falls 44.0 to 20.0, at every one of the five year-steps, while the number of children with a plan goes 244 to 238. The difference between the two therefore goes from 13.0 to 47.0 FTE. **WHAT IS ESTABLISHED is that the two published series diverge.** WHAT IS NOT is why: paraprofessionals moving onto general education assignments, the same people being recoded, and a change in what the state’s special education staff table counts all produce this shape, and subtracting one file from the other assumes the second sits inside the first, which nothing published says. This matters because the town’s own in-district special education escalator is built on a paraprofessional budget line. — closes: Lunenburg’s EPIMS work assignment detail by job classification and program area, year by year, which would show whether the same people were reported under a different code.

rows.what: What Lunenburg’s counsellors, social workers and psychologists do, as a series
rows.why: None of them is a teacher on DESE’s teacher returns, so the FTE files that carry fifteen years of teaching staff carry none of these people. The state’s educator retention file reaches them for three years only (FY2021–FY2023), as headcount rather than FTE, and folds them into two residual buckets named `Other - Licensed` and `Other - Non-Licensed`. The town’s annual report rosters name them every year FY2011–FY2025 and carry no FTE, no funding source and no date within the year. **The district itself holds the missing instrument**: it told the School Committee on 6 December 2023, while deciding what to cut, that “Information is broken out to social worker caseloads by bui lding”. That document is not published. Public comment at the same board on 24 January 2024 named MassHealth reimbursement and outside agencies as ways to pay for the same work, which is why a count without a funding source cannot answer the question anybody is asking. — closes: the per-building social worker and adjustment counsellor caseload the district prepared for the FY2025 budget, with FTE and funding source, which is a records request rather than a download.

rows.what: Why fewer Lunenburg High students take a history or a language course than before SY2020
rows.why: Three DESE series move together for both subjects — teacher FTE, student places and the share of the school taking one — and the fall in each begins in the years the school closed and reopened. A staffing decision, a change in what the timetable allowed, and students choosing differently all fit the same three numbers, and the state files nothing that separates them. — closes: the district’s course-request tallies for each year — what students asked for beside what ran. The High School Principal told the School Committee on 6 March 2024 that courses are whittled away once student choices are entered, so the tally exists at the moment the decision is made and is not published.

rows.what: How many classes ran in each subject at Lunenburg Middle School and Lunenburg High before SY2017
rows.why: Every trend on /what-courses-actually-ran is read inside an era, because for four years — SY2013 to SY2016 — Thomas C Passios was closed and every remaining school held one grade band higher, with grade 8 in the high school building. Four subjects move by more than ten points of participation into those years and back out of them without anything changing about what a ninth to twelfth grader was offered. So the file cannot say what the schools as they are now offered before SY2017 — the schools as they are now did not exist. — closes: nothing published can. DESE files by school and the schools changed; the question is only answerable by grade, and the state’s class-size collection carries no grade inside a school.

rows.what: What share of a post any non-teaching adult in a school holds
rows.why: DESE publishes a full-time equivalent for TEACHERS at school level and for nobody else. There is no published FTE — in any file, in any year — for a paraprofessional, an administrator, a nurse, a counsellor, a custodian or a kitchen post at a named school in this town. The one job-class table DESE publishes (`dese_educator_workforce`) is DISTRICT-only and carries headcount rather than FTE. So a school panel can say Lunenburg High printed 64 names and that 35.8 full-time-equivalent TEACHING posts sat among them, and it cannot say what the other 28 names amount to. **The difference between a roster count and a teaching FTE is not part-timers** — it is everybody the FTE file does not cover. — closes: DESE’s EPIMS work-assignment detail by job classification and school, or the district’s own staffing plan stating FTE by building and post.

rows.what: Which school year a printed staff roster describes
rows.why: The rosters in the annual town reports carry no date, and the town’s own prose suggests the school section may run a year ahead of the cover. Three sentences in fifteen reports name a fall and a student count; matched against DESE’s October enrolment for the same school, two are closer to the year AFTER the report’s fiscal year and one to the year on the cover. So a roster labelled FY2024 may describe the autumn of 2024, which the state calls FY2025 — and any children-per-adult figure drawn from the two may be a year out of step. The FY2024 report makes the hazard concrete: it prints two complete Turkey Hill rosters, 33 names in common, one naming the leadership the town printed in FY2025 and the other the leadership it printed from FY2011 to FY2022, and neither page says which year it is. — closes: a dated staff roster, or the district’s October 1 EPIMS submission, either of which states the day the count was taken.

rows.what: How much of what was said in a public meeting does a search of the archive actually reach?
rows.why: Our own text extraction inserts spaces inside words, at scale -- `w ell`, `s elling`, `dep artment`, `B oard` are all in the extracted minutes. Nine of the eleven hits for `ELL` are this rather than English learners. It costs twice: it manufactures tokens that were never printed, and -- the part that matters -- it makes PHRASE SEARCH MISS, because `study hall` broken as `study h all` will not match `"study hall"`. So a search that returns nothing may mean the words were said and our copy cannot be read, which is the exact failure the coverage denominator exists to prevent, arriving underneath it. The rate has not been measured and neither has the phrase-search undercount; both are countable against the source PDFs. This belongs to `extract_minutes.py`, not to the index. -- closes: nothing anybody publishes. A re-extraction with a layout-aware reader, measured against the same PDFs, is the only thing that settles it.

rows.what: Which school a Lunenburg student who left went to, by grade
rows.why: DESE publishes two files that each hold half of this and never the join. `dese_attrition` gives an attrition rate for every grade, every year, and names no destination. `dese_residents_sending` names every receiving district and the reason -- Monty Tech, school choice, charter, foster care -- and carries no grade at all. So the single largest measured departure in this town, about one in five of every eighth grade, cannot be attributed to anywhere: a vocational admission, a private school, a charter, a school choice transfer, an out-of-district placement and a family moving out of town are one number. — closes: one column. DESE's residents-sending file with a grade on each row, or the district's own October SIMS submission broken out by exit grade and exit reason, which the district files to the state every 1 October and does not report to its own School Committee.

rows.what: Why one in five Lunenburg eighth graders does not return for grade 9
rows.why: The rate is measured and stable across seventeen years, two building reorganisations and a pandemic. The reason is not measured anywhere. Monty Tech admits at grade 9 and Lunenburg is a member town there, so a child going there moves part of the town's bill rather than adding to it -- but nothing published links the two quantities, and the same rate is equally consistent with private and parochial admission at grade 9, with charter admission, with an out-of-district special education placement made at the transition, and with families moving. — closes: nothing anybody currently publishes. The nearest thing is an exit survey or an exit-reason tally kept by the district at the point a student is withdrawn, which is a record the district could choose to keep and report and does not.

rows.what: How many of the children counted as leaving a Lunenburg school moved out of town
rows.why: Attrition is leaving for ANY reason, so a family that moves to another state and a family that keeps its address and enrolls a child elsewhere are the same number. Without the split, the rate cannot be read as a statement about the schools at all -- and it is the reading every resident supplies. The town's own records could bound it: residency is what the district verifies at enrollment and what the assessor's and clerk's records track. — closes: the district's withdrawal records coded by reason (moved out of district / transferred within Massachusetts / private / home school), which is a field SIMS already requires the district to report on every exit.

rows.what: Who actually lives in Lunenburg — how many are over 65, how many households have a child in the schools, and what each group can afford?
rows.why: ANSWERED IN PART, 11 September 2026, and the part that remains is the part the argument actually runs on. The Census tables named below were fetched and are loaded as `census_acs`: 11,804 ± 19 residents, 1,979 ± 309 of them 65 or over, 4,529 ± 235 households, 1,477 ± 198 with a child under 18, median household income $109,753 ± $12,275 and $72,935 ± $8,677 where the householder is 65 or over. See /lunenburg-by-the-numbers, where every figure carries its margin. WHAT SURVIVES is the third clause — what each group can AFFORD. Income is not wealth, not savings, not equity and not a tax bill, and nothing published joins a property tax payment to the age of the person who paid it; the two rows below carry the two halves of what is still missing. — closes: the town census, which counts every resident by name, age and household rather than sampling them, held by the Town Clerk.

rows.what: How many Lunenburg homes have a child in the LUNENBURG PUBLIC SCHOOLS — as opposed to a child under 18?
rows.why: The Census answers the second and not the first. B11005 puts 1,477 of 4,529 households — 32.6% — with a child under 18, which is what people mean when they say "about 30% of taxpaying homes", and on that reading the claim is fair. But that count includes children at Monty Tech, at private and charter schools, and children not yet of school age, so it is a CEILING rather than the figure. The arithmetic suggests the gap is real: 1,477 households against roughly 1,745 school-age children is about 1.2 per household, low enough that a meaningful share of those homes have only pre-school children. Nothing published joins a child to a household to a school. — closes: a count of DISTINCT HOUSEHOLDS with at least one child enrolled, which the district can produce from its own student information system and DESE cannot, because DESE counts children and the Census counts households and neither knows about the other.

rows.what: How much of the property tax levy is paid by households headed by someone 65 or over?
rows.why: The Census now gives income by age of householder — a household headed by someone 65 or over has a median income of $72,935 ± $8,677, against $129,183 ± $21,150 for a 45-to-64 household — and that is income, not tax. The override argument is about a BILL: what a $3,000,000 override adds to a household is quoted at meetings as a town-wide average, and the town publishes no split of the levy by who pays it, by age or by anything else. Nor does it publish how many households take the statutory elderly exemptions and abatements that would change the answer. So "seniors on fixed incomes cannot carry it" cannot be checked in either direction, and neither can its opposite. — closes: the Board of Assessors’ commitment list with the Clause 41A, 41C and 17D exemptions granted, joined to the town census by age of owner — both held by the Town and neither published.

rows.what: How many school employees are enrolled in the district’s active health insurance, and on which plan tiers?
rows.why: NARROWED 5 October 2026. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include a school department presentation whose second page counts active subscribers by plan for FY26 budgeting: HMO Blue family 110, HMO Blue individual 32, Blue Care Elect family 19, individual 9, Blue Select 1 -- 171 in all. A district slide, not the carrier's census; the per-employee sheet behind it is held privately and not cited. The $3,701,195 FY2026 active line is the largest piece of the schools’ $5.22M health insurance and no document states its headcount. The Town Manager’s FY27 Unclassified presentation (12 March 2026, pp. 6–7) gives the town side to the person — 55 town actives, 67 town retirees, 203 school retirees, November 2025 enrollment — and the school active side only as a method (FY25 Superintendent’s budget update, p. 41: “counting all staff currently subscribing”). Subscribers are not people covered: a family plan is one subscriber. — closes: the MIIA renewal census by plan tier for the school department, or the PEC negotiation packet; both exist and neither is published.

rows.what: How many administrators does the district employ, and how has that changed over ten years?
rows.why: The annual-report rosters carry names without FTE, classify department liaisons as administrators, and print no central office at all in FY2025, so a series read off them shows administration falling by a quarter in a year in which nothing of the kind happened; DESE publishes administration only as dollars per pupil. — closes: the district’s position control list by FTE and funding source, for any two years ten apart.

rows.what: How many students played a school sport in each of the last ten years?
rows.why: The district has published season participation counts for three years (FY2024–FY2026), and the archive holds no earlier ones; a ten-year trend in athletes cannot be drawn. — closes: the athletic department’s season participation reports for FY2016–FY2023, which the department compiles each season.

rows.what: Are long-tenured homeowners being taxed out — what do households who bought decades ago earn against what they pay?
rows.why: The Census publishes tenure (B25038) and income by age of householder (B19049) but never the two together for a town this size; the assessor publishes the bill per parcel and nothing about the household. — closes: Census PUMS microdata for the PUMA containing Lunenburg, which carries tenure, year moved in and income per household, at the cost of covering several towns at once.

rows.what: Where was the schools’ FY2024 employee insurance reported, if not in the school department’s End of Year Financial Report?
rows.why: NARROWED 5 October 2026, and possibly reframed. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include a general fund budget-vs-actual history that carries the school department's active health insurance inside the SCHOOL general fund in every year FY2010-FY2025: account 0100-3-300-5200-99-1-99-2-570001, FY2024 actual 3,212,078.37 (sheet `School Only`, row 396). A Budget Master note records '$1,522,236 SHIFTED TO SCHOOL DEPT.' at FY2003 to FY2004. Why the EOYR total differs is not established. DESE’s EOYR shows function 5200 Insurance for Active Employees at $485,010 in FY2024 against $3,286,872 in FY2023 and $3,511,566 in FY2025; a difference read across that year looks like a $3M rise and is a reporting gap closing. Whether the year was mis-filed or the town appropriated and reported the insurance outside the school department is not established. — closes: the district’s FY2024 EOYR as submitted, Schedule 1, and the town’s FY2024 appropriation for group insurance by department.

rows.what: Which fund and account each field-rental receipt from Lunenburg Youth Soccer was posted to, and whether the $15,000 turf contribution is inside or beside them
rows.why: The district’s records-request answer lists seven receipts, FY2024–FY2026, $39,073.50 in all, with one MUNIS reference; the town’s FY26 special-revenue report carries fund 1306 School Facilities Use Revolving and fund 1545 Artificial Turf Revolving as balances only — closes: the journal detail export for funds 1306 and 1545, FY2024–FY2026, the same report the archive holds for fund 1301

rows.what: What Parks & Recreation’s programme fees and beach-pass sales became on the town’s books — how much of the $38,955.50 of programme fees and $8,828.00 of passes MyRec recorded for FY2025 reached fund 1500 (Park Revolving) or the general fund, and when
rows.why: MyRec is the registration system, not the ledger: its FY2025 sales reports foot to their own totals but say nothing about deposits, refunds or the fund each fee was posted to, and the FY2025 special-revenue report is not in the archive — closes: the FY2025 special-revenue report and the journal detail for fund 1500, the same report the archive holds for fund 1301.

rows.what: What each of the town’s 500-odd accounting measures did before FY2026, line by line — the appropriation history of every department and the year-by-year activity of every fund
rows.why: The registry (fund-owners.csv) lists every measure the FY26 reports print, but only the special-revenue funds have a read, tied history (FY2011–FY2023); the appropriation lines’ history sits in the annual reports where the extract cannot yet say which printed column is which, and FY2024–FY2025 fund activity was never printed — closes: the year-to-date budget reports and special-revenue reports for FY2023–FY2025 from the Town Accountant.

rows.what: When the town actually POSTED each agenda and each set of minutes — the two timestamps the Open Meeting Law turns on (48 hours of notice; minutes in a timely way)
rows.why: The AgendaCenter publishes no posting timestamp and our watch was seeded on 8 September 2026, so only 24 of 12,089 documents have a first-seen date. The documents’ own creation timestamps (sources/data/meeting-document-timestamps.csv) bound the posting from below and cannot prove when a file went up, and a file replaced in place takes a new date — closes: an AgendaCenter export carrying the posted-on date per document, or the town’s own record of when each was uploaded.

rows.what: What Lunenburg’s Chapter 32B §19 Public Employee Committee agreement actually sets — the premium split, the opt-out payment, and the plan menu
rows.why: CLOSED 6 October 2026 for FY27–FY29. The memorandum of agreement (`sources/contracts/pdf/pec-agreement-fy27-fy29.pdf`, 5 October) sets the plan menu, in-network cost-sharing, the HSA contribution, the $96 Medicare Part B reimbursement and the splits — 75/25 for active plans and Managed Blue for Seniors, 50/50 for Medex — 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2029. Its two blank attachments arrived on 6 October from the Town’s Human Resources Director, who wrote that ""The Benefit Summaries are Attachment A, and the Opt-Out Policy is Attachment B"": four Blue Cross summaries of benefits for the four active plans (`pec-fy27-attachment-a-1` to `-4`) and the FY27 opt-out guidelines (`pec-fy27-attachment-b-opt-out-policy.pdf`), which pay $3,000 for individual coverage, $6,000 for family and $3,000 for a change from family to individual. Still open: summaries for the two Medicare plans, registered separately. — closes: closed by the documents named.

rows.what: What the town’s 2020 post-65 Medicare transfer actually saved
rows.why: The town states it cut the active renewal 2% and reduced OPEB liability by $5–6M; both are figures in a budget presentation with no actuarial valuation behind them in the archive, and c.32B §20A means a valuation exists — closes: the OPEB valuation filed with PERAC for the year of the transfer.

rows.what: Whether the schools’ stated field and grounds costs match the books — about $126,000 of grounds work in FY2024 and $38,100 of outsourced mowing and field repair, paid, the Superintendent says, from the same revolving fund the field rent goes into
rows.why: The figures are the district’s own, read back from FY24 budget requests in an email of September 2026, and nothing in the archive tests them: fund 1306’s FY2024 expenditure is not published and the fund’s journal is not held — closes: the journal detail for fund 1306, FY2024–FY2026, and the FY2024 and FY2025 special-revenue reports.

rows.what: What put $62,231 into the School Facilities Use fund (1306) in FY2025 — the balance went from $3,010.67 at 30 June 2024 to $65,241.82 at 30 June 2025, more than the fund has taken in in any of the thirteen years the annual reports print
rows.why: Rent alone cannot produce the rise: the best receipts year on record is $39,944. Either revenue arrived that is not field rent — a transfer, a reimbursement, an insurance recovery — or something that had been charged to the fund stopped being charged to it, and the two balances cannot tell those apart. FY2025 is the one year no special-revenue schedule is published for. THE TEST WHEN THE DATA ARRIVES: read FY2025 line by line, total the receipts that are field or building rent, and see whether the remainder is a transfer in or an expenditure that moved elsewhere — closes: the journal detail for fund 1306, FY2024–FY2026, and the FY2025 special-revenue report.

rows.what: How much of each earlier year’s ski team cost was Lunenburg’s, and how much the other co-op towns’?
rows.why: The district’s by-sport workbook prints one figure for the ski team and it is the whole four-town co-op’s cost — $12,984 in FY2025, $10,960 in FY2024. The only invoice held is the 2025-26 one, where Lunenburg’s share was 21.4%. Nothing says any earlier year split the same way, or that the co-op had the same members — closes: the co-op invoices for the earlier seasons, which the athletic department issues and holds

rows.what: Where do the other towns’ ski co-op reimbursements land when they are paid?
rows.why: Lunenburg bills Littleton, Narragansett and Leominster for their skiers’ shares — $9,736.57 for 2025-26 — and which account receives the money decides whether it offsets the athletics line, the athletic revolving fund, or general revenue. The invoice is a bill and does not show receipt — closes: the revenue detail for the account the checks are deposited to, or the athletic revolving fund cashbook for the season

rows.what: What is in the PEC agreement that sets the town’s health insurance split and terms?
rows.why: NARROWED 6 October 2026. The PEC Agreement of 16 June 2008 is held (`sources/contracts/pdf/pec-agreement-2008.pdf`, a 16-page scan holding the 8-page agreement twice), received from the Town’s Human Resources Director by email. It names BCBS plans, a 75% Town share on the PPO, 80% then 75% from 1 July 2011 on the HMO and the two senior plans, 50% on Medex, 75% of the Medicare Part B premium, and a term of 1 July 2008 to 30 June 2012 continuing ""until the new agreement is reached"". What sits BETWEEN it and the FY27 memorandum, which amends ""the current in-force health insurance agreement"" without naming it, is not held: the Select Board minutes record ""the amendment dated May 14, 2013"" and a further amendment approved 11 March 2014, an agreement expiring 30 June 2016 (10 May 2016), and a Public Employee Agreement approved 12 April 2022 ""effective July 1, 2022"". Which of these the FY27 memorandum amends is not established. — closes: the complete, current agreement the Human Resources Director wrote on 6 October 2026 she was ""working on producing"", or the 2013, 2014, 2016 and 2022 instruments themselves. DECIDED 6 October 2026 (TJ): the current terms are modelled from the FY27 memorandum and its Attachments A and B, which restate every money term in full -- plans, the 75/25 and 50/50 splits, the $96 Part B payment, the $3,000/$6,000 opt-out, and the term to 30 June 2029. The missing instruments do not change any figure the model uses. They matter for the HISTORY of the split (when it moved, and to what) and for the procedural terms the memorandum carries over unrestated (eligibility, retiree and spouse definitions). Lower priority; ask when convenient.

rows.what: What do the two Medicare plans in the FY27–FY29 PEC agreement cover?
rows.why: The FY27 memorandum names six plans and puts ""benefit brochures"" in Attachment A; the Attachment A received on 6 October 2026 holds four, all for active plans (Network Blue New England, Network Blue Select, Access Blue New England Saver, Blue Care Elect). Managed Blue for Seniors and Medex — the plans the memorandum sets at 75/25 and 50/50 for retirees — have only their prescription copays stated in the memorandum itself. — closes: the MIIA summaries of benefits for Managed Blue for Seniors with PDP and Medex with PDP, FY27.

rows.what: Did the town ever adopt c.32B §§21–23, the expedited plan-design route?
rows.why: This decides whether plan design here is bargained in full or changed through 30 days and a binding panel. §21(a) makes it a vote of the board of selectmen in a town, so Town Meeting warrants were never the place to look; no such vote has been found in the Select Board record we hold. The Board was walked through the reform and its "Maximum Possible Savings" on 22 January 2013 and the follow-ups went to executive session. — closes: the Select Board vote adopting or declining §§21–23, or a statement that none exists.

rows.what: What was actually said in the 232 executive sessions the Select Board entered citing collective bargaining?
rows.why: 624 Select Board documents mention executive session and 232 cite collective bargaining; NO executive session minutes are in this archive. Health insurance is bargained there, so the open-session minutes catch the PEC only in passing — a phrase, an agenda line, a date — and never its substance. — closes: released executive session minutes, which the Open Meeting Law requires once the reason for secrecy has passed.

rows.what: Would regionalising change what the state sends Lunenburg, and by how much?
rows.why: This is among the most common arguments made about the deficit and the archive cannot price it. Regional districts receive regional transportation reimbursement under c.71 s16C that single-town districts do not, and no figure for it is held for any district. Per-pupil SPENDING is held and is a different quantity: it says what a district spends, not what the state sends. - closes: the Cherry Sheet regional transportation line for a comparable regional district, and DESE guidance on how the Chapter 70 formula treats a newly regionalised district.

rows.what: What did Ayer and Shirley each spend for each pupil BEFORE they regionalised?
rows.why: Ayer and Shirley regionalised for FY2012, which is the one local case anybody could learn from. The archive holds `Ayer` for FY2009-FY2011 and `Ayer Shirley School District` from FY2012, and nothing for Shirley alone beforehand - so the figure before is one town and the figure after is two. That is a different denominator, not a measured change, and comparing them would produce a confident number about the wrong thing. - closes: DESE per-pupil expenditure for Shirley, FY2009-FY2011.

rows.what: Is account 8129 the Zoning Incentive Stabilization Fund or the playground fund?
rows.why: The annual reports print 8129 as ZONING INCENTIVE STABILIZATION (TD BANKNORTH) in FY2020 and as Zoning Stabilization Fund in FY2025. This project’s own account registry, sources/data/fund-owners.csv, records 8129 as the playground fund with its owner unresolved. Both cannot be right, and the registry is what several pages read to name an account. The extracted balances keep the document’s name and flag the disagreement rather than resolving it. — closes: the Treasurer’s chart of accounts, or the Town Meeting article that created 8129.

rows.what: What spending the general Stabilization Fund would do to the town’s borrowing
rows.why: The town’s reserves are one of the things a rating agency weighs, and this archive holds NO bond rating for Lunenburg, no rating report, and no official statement from any bond issue — so what the rating is, what any agency has said about the reserves, and what a downgrade would cost per million borrowed are all unknown here. The question is live and has been asked in public: at the Finance Committee on 13 March 2025 a resident asked whether not contributing to OPEB affects the town’s bond rating, and the minutes record the question and no reply. Until this closes, any sentence about "what the rating agencies would think" is a hypothesis, including on /analysis/stabilization-option, which says so. — closes: the official statement for the town’s most recent bond issue, and the rating agency report that accompanied it, both of which the Treasurer holds.

rows.what: Whether Lunenburg has a written reserve target, and what it is
rows.why: NARROWED 5 October 2026. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include a Free Cash Fact Sheet for the FY27 warrant quoting the Town of Lunenburg Free Cash Policy, Section 3.03 (amended 09/02/2014 and 10/18/2018). That is a quotation of the policy, not the adopted policy document, which remains the remedy. Nothing in this archive states a level the town intends to keep in stabilization or free cash — no reserve policy, no fund balance policy, no target as a share of the operating budget. So there is no stated floor any drawdown could be measured against, and "the reserves are healthy" and "the reserves are excessive" are both unfalsifiable here. The Finance Committee has had "Financial Related Policies" as standing Old Business (agenda, 10 September 2026) and funded a financial policies line, so a document may exist or be in progress. — closes: the town’s adopted financial reserve policy, or the Finance Committee’s confirmation in writing that none has been adopted.

rows.what: What each town department was appropriated and spent in FY2024 and FY2025
rows.why: NARROWED 5 October 2026 for FY2024. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include a general fund budget-vs-actual history for every department, FY2010-FY2025, by MUNIS account (original, transfers, revised, actual). Its FY2025 column is part-year, so FY2025 stays open. Special revenue funds are not in it. The town published a General Fund Appropriations / Summary & Classification of Accounts schedule in every annual report through FY2023 — every department, appropriated against expended, with a printed GRAND TOTAL — and STOPPED. Its own contents pages show it: the FY2023 Accountant section lists the schedule and the General Fund Revenue and Expenditures charts; FY2024 lists a balance sheet, receivables, special revenue, capital, enterprise, trust and undesignated fund balance, and no appropriations at all; FY2025 is shorter again. FY2024 still prints the warrant’s FY 2025 Omnibus Budget, which is what was VOTED and not what was spent; FY2025 prints no department figures in any form, only Article 10’s total of $49,374,465.00 split across five funding sources. So for two consecutive years there is no published answer to what any single department was given or used — the question this archive answers for FY2011 through FY2023. — closes: the Town Accountant’s general fund appropriation and expenditure report for FY2024 and FY2025, the same schedule the annual report printed through FY2023, or the MUNIS year-end expense report by department for those years.

rows.what: How many people each TOWN department employs, in FTE, in a form that can be counted the same way twice
rows.why: CORRECTED. This row previously said the only published series stops at FY2016, when the gross-wages list stopped tagging each name with a department. That is true of the WAGE LIST and it is not true of the reports. Every annual report carries departments describing their own staffing in the prose of their narrative section -- 77 such statements across FY2011 to FY2025, in every year. The Fire Department gives a series on its own: 5 Career and 40-45 On Call in FY2017, 7 Career from FY2018, 10 Career and 30-35 On Call/Per Diem from FY2022. The DPW states its establishment post by post: one Director, one Executive Assistant shared with Facilities, one Highway Superintendent, 5 Heavy Equipment Operators, one Mechanic, one Cemetery Superintendent, two Seasonal Cemetery Laborers, one Sewer Business Manager and one Assistant. The Building Department, the Council on Aging and the Assessor's office do the same. WHAT REMAINS A GAP is that none of it is FTE and none of it is consistent: a range (30-45 on call), a headcount, and a list of titles are three different quantities, stated in whichever form that year's department head chose, and they cannot be summed into a town total or compared like for like across departments. -- closes: the town's payroll register by department, or the personnel schedule behind the omnibus budget, which sets an FTE per line before Town Meeting votes it.

rows.what: Whether a department cut SERVICE, as opposed to cutting dollars or people
rows.why: A budget line that falls is not a cut and a headcount that falls is not a service reduction -- the thing a resident notices is hours, response times, programmes and waits. The annual reports do carry that: every year's department narratives print activity statistics such as calls for service, items circulated, patron visits, permits issued and inspections performed. None of it is extracted, and it is prose rather than tables, which is the same reason fifteen years of out-of-district placement counts went unread. Until it is read, no claim that a department held its service level while another cut can be tested in either direction. -- closes: nothing external is needed. This one is ours to do -- the figures are already in documents the archive holds.

rows.what: How many people work in the offices voted as General Government — the Town Manager, the Town Clerk, the Treasurer/Collector and Information Technology
rows.why: Nine town departments now state a headcount somewhere in their own report, but General Government is voted as ONE figure covering several offices and only the Assessing office inside it states a number. Health & Sanitation, Central Purchasing, Solid Waste and Employee benefits state none at all. The gross-wages list named a department beside each employee through FY2016 and stopped — closes: the Town’s gross wages list with its department column restored, or any payroll headcount by department.

rows.what: What each town department spends on wages, so departments can be compared by payroll rather than by headcount
rows.why: The town prints a `Town & School Employee Gross Wages` list every year, name by name — but it stopped printing the DEPARTMENT beside each name after FY2016, so the list cannot be split by department. Joining the names to the rosters we hold matches only a third to a half of them, so any departmental total built this way would rank our reading of the scan rather than the town’s payroll. THE REASON RECORDED HERE UNTIL 28 SEPTEMBER 2026 WAS WRONG: it said the two-column layout loses the second column’s given names, which was a measurement of OUR OCR CACHE written down as a fact about the town’s typesetting. The FY2019 pages print both columns in full, and a re-read lifted that year from 44 names to 516 in `gross-wages.csv`, and a reading of the pages themselves on 2 October 2026 found the pages print 599 -- so 83 names are in no dataset, 65 of them on PDF page 200 alone. 516 was a count of OUR dataset; 599 is a count of the town’s page. Nothing from it is published for that reason — closes: the wage list with its department column restored, or any payroll report by department.

rows.what: How much of a department’s headcount is full-time
rows.why: A roster counts the Council on Aging's Tuesday van driver and its Director as one each. ONE FTE FIGURE DOES EXIST and this row used to deny it: the FY2025 Finance Committee report states the FY2026 school budget “necessitates eliminating approximately 28 Full-Time Equivalents (39 employees)”, which also measures the gap between posts and people — 39 people in 28 FTE. That is one department in one year; no FTE is published for any other department or any other year — closes: an FTE schedule, or the wage list read in full.

rows.what: Whether a fall in a department’s headcount is a post being cut or a post standing empty
rows.why: A roster is people IN post; a cut removes a POST. The two come apart both ways — somebody leaves a funded post and the count falls with nothing cut, or a post is eliminated and its holder moves into another vacancy so the count holds. The Assessing office reported being “fully staffed for the first time in over a year” in FY2024, which is a year of posts that existed and stood empty and would have read here as a smaller department. Only the DPW and the Assessing office publish an establishment at all — closes: an authorised-post schedule, or a vacancy report, for any department.

rows.what: Who chaired each town board after FY2016?
rows.why: the officials listing marked its chairs with `** denotes chairperson` and stopped printing the footnote after FY2016; 46 bodies name a chair somewhere in their own report and 53 do not, so 218 body-years have members and nobody at the top — closes: the Town Clerk’s record of board organisational votes, which every board takes annually

rows.what: Which town posts are funded but standing empty?
rows.why: a roster names who is there and an establishment names the posts, and only the DPW and the Assessing office publish the second — so a department that shrank and a department that could not hire look identical. The Police Department’s FY27 budget presentation marks every post `Funded` or `Funded – Vacant`, which is exactly the distinction, for one department in one year — closes: the FY27 budget presentations for every department, if they all mark posts that way

rows.what: Who appoints each appointed official, and to whom do they answer?
rows.why: the annual report heads six pages `APPOINTED OFFICIALS` and names nobody as the appointing authority, so a Constable, a Town Clockwinder and a Wellness Coordinator sit in the record with no department and no stated superior. The town charter is the document that says which appointments belong to the Select Board and which to the Town Manager, and this archive does not hold it — closes: the Lunenburg town charter and the general bylaws

rows.what: Who works in Accounting, Human Resources, Land Use and Facilities?
rows.why: the town’s own staff directory lists 29 departments and these four are in none of this project’s 61 bodies — a department that files no annual report is absent from the contents page, and one whose head is not an APPOINTED OFFICIAL is absent from the officials listing, so both our sources miss the same four. The Facilities Director is named in the FY2023 report and on the Town Office Hours page and appears in no roster — closes: the town staff directory at lunenburgma.gov/directory.aspx, whose PEOPLE tab names everyone by department

rows.what: Who are the ten people the Public Library employs?
rows.why: the Library told the town in FY2019 that it employs ten — *“we only employ ten total”* — and it has never printed a roster. Its annual report is signed by the Director and names a colleague only in passing prose (a Young Adult Services Librarian in FY2024, a Digital Services Librarian the same year), so the org chart holds ONE of ten. The town staff directory does not carry the Library at all: it is governed by elected Trustees rather than run from Town Hall, and has no category on lunenburgma.gov — closes: the Library’s own staff page, or the Trustees’ minutes, which record appointments

rows.what: Why does the town open FY2018 owed $13,300 more than it closed FY2017 owing?
rows.why: THE TOWN PRINTS BOTH FIGURES AND THEY DO NOT MEET. A receivable balance rolls forward: what the town was owed on 30 June is what it starts the next year owed. Every other consecutive pair we can read ties to the cent (FY2020 through FY2024, one pair off by 2c). The Collector’s grand total on FY2017 page 45 reads $9,008,228.35 and on FY2018 page 54 reads $9,021,528.35 — checked on the pages, not off our extract. A prior-year adjustment, a reclassified charge and a typo all fit it equally and nothing published distinguishes them. — closes: the Collector’s receivable control reconciliation for FY2018, which is a report the accounting system can print.

rows.what: What was Lunenburg's certified new growth in fiscal 2012?
rows.why: THE TOWN’S OWN REPORTS GIVE TWO FIGURES AND DISAGREE ABOUT WHICH YEAR EACH BELONGS TO. The FY2013 report prints $19,124,255 against fiscal 2012. The FY2014 through FY2017 reports print $27,729,619 against fiscal 2012 and re-date $19,124,255 to fiscal 2013. Nothing in the archive resolves which labelling is right, and new growth is what the levy limit grows by, so the two readings imply different ceilings. — closes: DOR’s LA-13 new growth certification for FY2012.

rows.what: What added valuation produced fiscal 2009's $138,168 of new growth?
rows.why: THE ARITHMETIC ON THE PAGE DOES NOT WORK AND FIVE EDITIONS REPRINT IT UNCHANGED. $5,077,276 of added valuation, at the $12.23 rate printed on the same line, gives $62,095 — not the $138,168 beside it. The report’s own percentage-change column corroborates $138,168, so the added-valuation figure is the one that cannot be right. Recorded rather than corrected: which of the two the town meant is not something this archive can say. — closes: DOR’s LA-13 new growth certification for FY2009.

rows.what: Why does the same $1,085,674.86 appear twice in the town’s FY2015 opening receivables?
rows.why: THE TOWN’S OWN TWO BOOKS DO NOT MEET, AND THE AMOUNT IS EXACT. FY2014 closes `MEADOW BETTERMENT` at $1,085,674.86. FY2015 opens `SEWER BETTERMENT` $1,085,674.86 higher than FY2014 closed it, AND carries the same $1,085,674.86 again on a new `MEADOW WOODS WATER BETT` line. Both years tie to their own printed GRAND TOTAL, and line by line every other balance rolls forward near-exactly. A recoding of Meadow Woods into the sewer betterment line would explain it; so would a restatement; nothing published distinguishes them. — closes: the town’s FY2015 receivable roll-forward, or the MUNIS receivable detail for both years.

rows.what: Whose $92,709.54 is the unnamed line in the FY2015 receivables summary?
rows.why: THE REPORT PRINTS A FIGURE ON A LINE WITH NO NAME. $92,709.54 in the PAYMENTS column, under `UTILITY LIENS ADDED TO TAXES`, with an empty name cell — confirmed by rendering page 45 rather than off the scan. Seven of the eight columns tie to the cent without it and PAYMENTS is short by exactly that amount, so the figure is real and the name is what is missing. Carried in the data as `(the page prints no name for this line)`. — closes: the Collector’s detail behind the FY2015 receivables summary.

rows.what: Does the town’s printed debt repayment grand total include all of its debt?
rows.why: IN THE FY2015 REPORT IT DOES NOT, BY THE EXACT AMOUNT OF TWO BONDS. The `GRAND TOTAL PRINCIPAL` row is short by the two MS-HS CONSTRUCTION bonds in every year column — $625,000 in 2016, $640,000 in 2017, $665,000 in 2018 — while both bonds are printed in the table directly above it. The school construction bonds are the second largest debt on the page. Nothing here establishes whether the row or the table is the intended figure. — closes: the Treasurer’s debt service schedule for FY2015, or the official statement for the MS-HS bonds.

rows.what: Which building a shared school employee actually works in, and for how much of the week
rows.why: Twenty-eight people are printed as staff by more than one Lunenburg school on the schools’ own listings, one of them by four of them. THAT REPETITION IS THE MEASUREMENT AND NOTHING MORE: it is consistent with a specialist splitting a week between two buildings, with a district post housed in one school and serving all of them, and with two buildings both claiming somebody neither employs alone — and the documents do not separate those. The district’s roll-up encodes sharing a second way, in a free-text column that reads `Primary School & THES`, and the two encodings agree about five of the 28. Neither carries a fraction, so `Carol Saranich`, listed by the high school, the middle school and Turkey Hill, could be a third of a post in each or a full post in one. This is rule 11 pointed at people: a name on a list is not a share of a job, and the budget lines that pay for these posts are netted and per-district, so they cannot be split by building either. — closes: the district’s FTE-by-building assignment schedule, the sheet behind the personnel lines in the school budget.

rows.what: When an agenda was actually POSTED, and so whether a meeting had its 48 hours’ notice
rows.why:
The Open Meeting Law requires 48 hours’ notice excluding weekends and holidays, and NOTHING THE TOWN PUBLISHES SAYS WHEN AN AGENDA WENT UP. Checked rather than assumed: the AgendaCenter listing that every agenda is fetched from was searched in full for `posted`, `published`, `uploaded`, `created` and `modified`, and for any date-bearing attribute — zero occurrences of any of them. The row carries the MEETING date and nothing else.

Two things stand in for it and neither is the answer. A PDF’s own creation timestamp is a LOWER BOUND on posting, since a file cannot be posted before it is made — the School Committee Policy Sub-Committee agenda of 25 September 2026 was created at 14:29 the previous afternoon, so the most notice possible for that file was 19 hours, and whether that is the notice actually given is not established. The AgendaCenter also allows a file to be replaced in place, so an earlier version could have been posted earlier and overwritten.

And our own `first_seen` is worse, because it measures US. The watcher did not run on 18, 22 or 24 September 2026, so a document first seen on the 25th could have been posted on any of three days. A gap in the crawl silently becomes a gap in what can be said. — closes: the AgendaCenter’s posting log, which CivicEngage records internally and the site does not display; the Town Clerk can produce it.

rows.what: Which towns does Lunenburg consider comparable to itself, for tax and budget purposes?
rows.why: This project compares Lunenburg with five peer towns and that set is OURS. Nothing the town has published names a cohort: a 2023 Finance Committee minute cites "the 8 communities that were surveyed" for a salary study and never lists them, and no budget document, capital plan or assessors’ report names a comparison group. So every "compared with similar towns" statement on either side rests on a set nobody has agreed. — closes: the eight-community list behind the 2023 salary survey, which the Town Administrator or the bargaining unit that commissioned it holds.

rows.what: How is a regional school district’s assessment apportioned between its member towns, and what does each town actually appropriate for schools?
rows.why: NARROWED 26 September 2026. This used to say a regional town could not be compared at all. That was asking at the wrong level: Chapter 70 is computed per MUNICIPALITY whatever district its children attend, so DESE publishes, for all 351 towns, the foundation budget for that town’s own children, the contribution the town is REQUIRED to make and by subtraction what the state adds — Ashby is required to raise $7,819 per child, Groton $10,748, Lunenburg $8,571. What is still unpublished is the step between: how the district divides its assessment among members, and what each member town actually appropriates, which may be well above the required minimum. — closes: each regional district’s annual assessment schedule, voted by its member towns’ meetings and filed with DESE.

rows.what: What does Lunenburg pay, per child, for each place a resident child is schooled outside the district’s own schools?
rows.why: DESE publishes WHERE Lunenburg children are enrolled — 177 outside the district in FY2026 — and nothing about what any of them costs. A count of children is not a tuition, a charter assessment or a share of a regional assessment, and the general fund budget shows the appropriation rather than the fund each payment leaves. So the two halves of the question a resident actually asks — how many leave, and what that costs us — cannot be joined. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for Lunenburg, which separates tuition and assessment spending by fund and by receiving district.

rows.what: What would regionalising actually be worth to Lunenburg, once the transport reimbursement is set against the transport costs it would also take on?
rows.why: NARROWED 26 September 2026, and half of it is now answered. The reimbursement side is measured: the DLS Cherry Sheet is in the archive, FY2010–FY2027, and Regional Transportation under M.G.L. c.71 s.16C is $88,183,608 statewide in FY2026 to 84 regional districts and nothing to any single-town district. North Middlesex draws $1,195,321, Ashburnham-Westminster $1,190,725, Groton-Dunstable $1,001,384. What is NOT answerable from any file is the other half: a regional district also INCURS the busing it is reimbursed for, and no published figure separates a district’s transport cost from its reimbursement — DESE’s twelve per-pupil categories carry no transport line at all. Nor is the counterfactual observable: what three towns would spend merged is not what other merged towns spend today. — closes: the regional districts’ own budgets, which state transportation as a line and the reimbursement against it; and a regional agreement, which sets how the net cost is apportioned.

rows.what: Which fund pays the teacher salaries a district charges to grants and revolving accounts?
rows.why: DESE’s function-code file splits spending into general fund and grants-plus-revolving, and the gap between comparable districts is large: Harvard charges $4,964 per pupil of TEACHER salaries to grants and revolving funds where Lunenburg charges $726. That single line is most of the difference in what the two draw from outside the appropriation. The file does not say WHICH fund — a specific grant, school choice tuition received, a tuition agreement — and the answer decides whether it is something Lunenburg could pursue or a feature of one district’s circumstances. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Pupil and Financial Report for the district, which reports spending by individual fund.

rows.what: How do Ipswich, Woburn, Lenox, Medford, Canton, Norwood fund schools in the top quarter of spending while taxing homes in the lightest quarter?
rows.why: Of the 20 towns that spend among the most per pupil while asking the least of a home’s value, 6 fit none of the four routes this report can test: an unusual amount of state aid, many houses per child, houses worth a great deal each, or an unusually large business base. Three of them — Woburn, Canton, Norwood — carry business shares of roughly twice the median and fail only the exact 2x test. Whatever the rest are doing is the most directly useful thing on this page and nothing here identifies it. — closes: DLS Schedule A for each town, which reports every revenue source a municipality collects, so local receipts, enterprise funds and reserves can be compared rather than inferred.

rows.what: Is a rate printed in a town salary schedule the rate that was paid, and is the schedule itself internally consistent?
rows.why: The Salary Administration Plan schedule voted at the 2022 annual town meeting -- page 152 of the FY2022 annual report -- prints 20 grades against 8 steps and NO TOTAL of any kind, so nothing on the page tests its own figures. Its 160 hourly rates sit about 3% apart step to step and no single rounding rule reproduces them: round(step 1 x 1.03^(n-1)) misses 50 of the 140 derived cells, and grade 2 step 2 computes 15.38 where the page prints 15.37. The reading is safe because the page carries its own text layer and the characters are exact, but the DOCUMENT has no internal check a reader could apply, and a typo in a published schedule would be invisible. Separately, the schedule says what a grade and step pay per hour and says nothing about who is in which grade, at which step, or for how many hours -- so it cannot be turned into what the town spent on anyone. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the printed rates are the rates the payroll system actually applied. -- closes: the Personnel Committee’s own rate table as submitted to the Town Clerk, which the warrant says is on file, read against the payroll register for the same year.

rows.what: Who is in which of the two lists the gross wage pages print, and is anyone in both?
rows.why: The `Calendar Year 2022 Gross Wages` pages (186-192 of the FY2022 annual town report) print TWO columns, and each is alphabetised A to Z independently all the way through the seven pages -- the left column runs ABRAHAM to ZRATE across 332 names and the right BIERY to YOURK across 329. Neither is a continuation of the other, and the document puts NO HEADING over either column and no total under either, so nothing in it says what separates the two. The obvious reading -- one is the town payroll and the other the school payroll -- is a HYPOTHESIS and nothing on the page tests it. It matters because a resident adding the two columns is adding two populations they cannot name, because several surnames appear in both columns, and because the list carries no department, no position and no hours for anyone: it is 661 names and 661 gross figures. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: what the two lists are, whether any person is counted in both, and which fund paid any of it. -- closes: the Town Accountant’s payroll register for calendar year 2022 with its department and fund coding, which is the report the wage list is printed from.

rows.what: What the Sewer Reserve Capacity and Arts Lottery funds held at 30 June 2023
rows.why: The FY2023 annual town report prints each of these balances TWICE, in two different tables, and the two printings disagree. `TRUST AND STABILIZATION FUNDS HELD BY OTHER BANKS` (pdf page 49) gives SEWER RESERVE CAPACITY (UNIBANK) an ENDING CASH VALUE of $28,144.20 and ARTS LOTTERY (MMDT) $19,120.90. `Treasurer's Cash as of 6/30/2023` (pdf page 48) gives Unibank Sewer Capacity Reserve Stabilization $28,144.50 and Mass Municipal Depository Trust (MMDT) Arts Lottery $19,121.07. NEITHER IS A MISREADING: each column foots to its own printed total to the cent -- page 49's eleven funds sum to the printed GRAND TOTALS of $2,363,536.23, and page 48's thirty-nine accounts sum to the printed Total Treasurer Cash of $27,244,162.79 -- so the report disagrees with itself by $0.30 and $0.17. Six other funds appear on both pages and match exactly, which is what makes the two the odd ones rather than the tables a different measure. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which of the two each pair is. An ending cash value on a custodian's trust statement and a treasurer's cash balance are produced by different parties on different books and the report relates them nowhere, so the difference may be a posting date, an accrual, or a typing error in one of them, and nothing here can tell those apart. The amounts are small; the pattern is not, because these two tables are the only two statements of these balances the town publishes and they are printed in every annual report. -- closes: the Treasurer's year-end reconciliation of cash to the custodian's statements at 30 June 2023, which the annual report does not contain.

rows.what: What was Lunenburg's certified assessed valuation and tax rate for fiscal 2021?
rows.why: THREE DOCUMENTS GIVE THREE ANSWERS AND NONE OF THEM IS THE TOWN'S OWN TABLE ADDING UP. The FY2021 annual report, page 38, prints four property classes totalling $1,742,668,758.00 under a Totals line that reads $1,548,256,450 -- and that Totals line, with its $28,054,406.88 levy, is to the cent the one the FY2020 report prints, where it foots FY2020's own four classes at FY2020's rate of 18.12. DLS's assessed-value series puts Lunenburg's FY2021 total at $1,628,643,589, which matches neither. And the rate is printed as 17.19 in every row of the table while the prose above it says the rate went from $18.12 to $17.74 for FY 2021. Until one of these is settled, no FY2021 valuation, levy or rate can be quoted from the annual report, and the class SHARES -- which /commercial-base is built on -- rest on a base the town does not state. The four class rows are internally consistent and are not in doubt: each one's valuation x 17.19 / 1000 is its own printed levy to the cent. — closes: the Division of Local Services Tax Rate Recapitulation (the certified recap, with the LA-4 assessed values) for Lunenburg, fiscal 2021, which DLS publishes per municipality per year on its Gateway/Municipal Databank.

rows.what: Which of the FY2021 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?
rows.why: The Treasurer's FY2021 receipts page (annual town report PDF p25) prints 100 line items in three free-form label/amount columns with NO column header, and a SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block of nine categories footing to a GRAND TOTAL of $44,252,049.61.
