Six of the nine categories are defined by a heading the page prints above the lines and each foots exactly -- licenses and permits, state revenue, special assessments, fines and forfeits, investment income, transfers from other funds. The other three print no heading that separates them, and their 60 lines foot as one block to $31,988,239.19. A residual does fit -- the taxes/interest/demands lines plus prior year excise and prior year interest, LESS supplemental tax on new construction, is $31,200,742.70 to the cent -- but that is arithmetic choosing a grouping rather than the document stating one, and other partitions fit the same three printed totals equally well. So we can say what the town took in, and not how it classified 60 of the lines. -- closes: the Treasurer's own receipts workbook for FY2021, the file the page is printed from, which carries the category each line is coded to. Not published; a records request to the Town Treasurer would obtain it.

rows.what: How many Montachusett foundation-enrolment students did Harvard have in FY2018 — 7 or 8?
rows.why: The FY2017 annual town report prints the figure twice and the two disagree by one student. Page 144 is DESE's own `FY18 Chapter 70 / Regional District Enrollment and Contributions by Member City or Town` for LEA 832 and prints HARVARD at 7; page 148 is the district's COMMUNITY ASSESSMENTS table and prints its FOUNDATION ENROLLMENT at 8. The two agree on all 17 other towns and on all 18 Required Minimum Contributions to the dollar. Only page 148's column foots to the District Total of 1,496 that BOTH pages print; page 144's 18 rows sum to 1,495, although its own per-row Change identities all close. Foundation enrolment is the input Chapter 70 runs on, so a member town's count is load-bearing for every town's assessment — and neither page says which of its own figures is the error. — closes: DESE's published FY18 Chapter 70 regional district enrolment file for LEA 832 Montachusett, at doe.mass.edu, which is the source both pages reproduce.

rows.what: Which department carried forward the $362.00 the FY2017 appropriations schedule does not print?
rows.why: The FY2017 GENERAL FUND APPROPRIATIONS schedule, pages 24-28 of the annual town report, states twice that a $362.00 carry-forward exists and never prints the line. Its APPROPRIATED FORWARD column sums to $37,626,083.44 against a printed GRAND TOTAL of $37,626,445.44, and its footer legend `fwd - forward from FY 2016 $637,981.43` exceeds the 26 fwd lines actually printed by the same $362.00 — while the srt and rft legend totals reproduce to the cent and the other three columns tie exactly. The subtotal for Police Fire Medical Expenses on page 25 is $5,362.00 over a single line item of $5,000.00, so the money belongs to that block; which prior-year appropriation it is a carry-forward OF is not stated anywhere in the document. The amount is trivial; the question is not, because the same schedule is the basis of every departmental growth rate this project measures and a carry-forward line changes which year a dollar belongs to. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2017 year-end MUNIS encumbrance and carry-forward detail, which lists each forwarded balance by account.

rows.what: Which of the FY2020 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?
rows.why: The Treasurer's FY2020 receipts page (annual town report PDF p24) prints 100 line items in three free-form label/amount columns with NO column header, and a SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block of nine categories footing to a GRAND TOTAL of $43,089,202.54. Both halves of the page were read off its own embedded bitmap on 2 October 2026 and both close to the cent: the 100 detail lines add to the GRAND TOTAL, and so, separately, do the nine summary lines. Six of the nine categories are defined by a heading the page prints above their lines and each foots exactly -- licenses and permits $331,254.75 (19 lines), state revenue $9,790,141.52 (12), special assessments $68,681.50 (3), fines and forfeits $37,182.61 (4), investment income $102,340.41 (1) and transfers from other funds $2,291,492.46 (1). The other three print no heading that separates them, and their 60 lines foot as ONE block to $30,468,109.29, the sum of the three printed category totals. A residual does fit -- moving SUPPL TAX-NEW CONSTRUCTION $10,057.81 out of taxes and $100,180.88 of RESCUE WAGON out of non-recurring would close all three -- but that is arithmetic choosing a grouping rather than the document stating one, and other partitions fit the same three printed totals equally well. So we can say what the town took in, and not how it classified 60 of the lines. This is the SAME gap already registered for FY2021 and it is a property of the form, not of one year. -- closes: the Treasurer's own receipts workbook for FY2020, the file the page is printed from, which carries the category each line is coded to. Not published; a records request to the Town Treasurer would obtain it.

rows.what: Does the FY2018 debt repayment schedule's printed grand total account for every issue's INTEREST?
rows.why: IN FY2019 IT DOES NOT, BY THE EXACT INTEREST OF ONE ISSUE. Pages 48-51 of the FY2018 annual town report print sixteen debt issues against FY2019-FY2047 and, separately, GRAND TOTAL rows per year. Read in full, the issues reconcile to those grand totals within $2 in all 29 years -- the schedule shows whole dollars over amounts carrying cents -- except FY2019, where the issues' interest exceeds the printed GRAND TOTAL INTEREST by 272 and TOTAL DEBT by the same 272 while principal ties EXACTLY. 272 is precisely the FY2019 interest of MASS WATER POOL 4*, whose own row closes to the dollar (10,409 + 272 = 10,681) and whose 10,409 of principal IS inside the grand total. So one of the two printed figures is wrong and the document does not say which; the archive publishes both and asserts neither. This is the same defect the FY2015 row in this register names for PRINCIPAL, in a different year and a different column, and the two may be worth merging. - closes: the Treasurer's own debt service schedule for FY2019, or the Massachusetts Clean Water Trust (formerly MWPAT) amortization schedule for Pool 4, either of which states that loan's FY2019 interest and admin fee independently of the town's own summary.

rows.what: Which figure did the 2018 Annual Town Meeting actually vote where the printed FY 2019 Omnibus Budget does not add up?
rows.why: The budget as printed on pages 155-158 of the FY2018 annual town report carries TWO arithmetic misprints and the document contradicts itself about both. `Total General Government $1,401,119.25` is 709.00 MORE than the 22 lines beneath it, and the printed `Total Omnibus $36,804,408.83` agrees with the subtotal rather than with the lines. `Total Assistance $243,493.56` is 2,000.00 LESS than the two subtotals above it, and there the Total Omnibus agrees with the subtotals rather than with the line. Ten of the twelve section totals foot their own line items to the cent, every subtotal foots exactly, and the pages carry a digital text layer, so this is the town's arithmetic and not our reading. What a resident cannot tell from the published report is which number was put to the meeting: the appropriation is voted as one sum, and a 709.00 or 2,000.00 difference changes what the departments beneath it were authorised to spend. - closes: the Town Clerk's certified record of the vote on Article 7 of the 5 May 2018 Annual Town Meeting, which states the sum voted and the schedule attached to it.

rows.what: Which fiscal year did Town Meeting vote the left-hand half of the FY 2016 Omnibus Budget for?
rows.why: The omnibus schedule on pages 140-141 of the FY2015 annual town report is titled `FY 2016 Omnibus Budget` and is set as two panels per page. Its right panel is headed `VOTED FY 2016` and its left panel `VOTED FY 2015`. Everything else on the page says it is one column: the line numbers run 1 to 82 continuously across both panels and both pages, the 91 line items sum exactly to the single TOTAL OMNIBUS of $32,025,895.00, and so do the twelve printed section totals. But the report itself never states which heading is wrong, and the arithmetic cannot tell a misprinted heading from a correct one. Until it is settled, no figure from the left panel may be cited as an FY2015 appropriation or as an FY2016 one without saying which. - closes: the Town Clerk's record of the vote at the 2015 Annual Town Meeting, with the warrant article and the amount as moved, which the town holds and does not publish.

rows.what: What was the Town owed in motor vehicle excise, user charges and betterments at 30 June 2016?
rows.why: THE FY2016 RECEIVABLES SUMMARY IS PRINTED CLIPPED, AND THE CLOSING COLUMNS ARE THE ONES CUT OFF. Page 47 of the FY2016 annual town report prints the property-tax half of the schedule with EIGHT columns -- FORWARD, COMMITTMENTS, ADJUSTMENTS, REFUNDS, PAYMENTS, ABATEMENTS, TRANSFER, BALANCES -- and every row closes on the identity those columns state. Page 48 (motor vehicle excise, twenty levy years) stops after PAYMENTS. Page 49 (deferred taxes, water and sewer user charges, utility liens, sewer/water/street/septic betterments, apportioned assessments) stops after REFUNDS, and its own title is cut mid-word -- `FY2016 COLLECTION OF TAXE`. Page 50 is blank but for its folio, so nothing continues. Both pages were rendered and looked at on 2 October 2026: the ruled table simply ends at the right-hand edge of the page. SO THERE IS NO PUBLISHED BALANCE for any of those accounts and no arithmetic on either page can be closed. The combined balance sheet on page 20 does not substitute: it prints one undivided `EXCISES $243,852.65` against page 48's five columns netting $303,306.05, which are not the same quantity. This is NOT the same gap as the FY2013/FY2017/FY2020 receivables refusals, which are about an extractor failing on pages that ARE fully printed -- here the document does not carry the figures. — closes: the Collector's and Treasurer's own FY2016 receivables control report, or an un-clipped printing of the same worksheet, which the Town Accountant's system can reproduce.

rows.what: What else did the Town receive in FY2016 after CH 70 SCHOOL AID, and what did its receipts add up to?
rows.why: THE FY2016 RECEIPTS PAGE IS CUT OFF MID-LIST AND PRINTS NO TOTAL. `FY 2016 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2016`, PDF page 23 of the annual town report, is a two-column list of about 54 figures. The left column ends at `RELEASE FEES` in the middle of the FEES block; the right column ends at `CH 70 SCHOOL AID` in the middle of the STATE REVENUE block. Both stop at the same height on the page, which is what a print that ran out of room looks like. There is no SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block and no GRAND TOTAL anywhere on it. The comparison is the Town's own later practice: the FY2020 and FY2021 receipts pages print about 100 detail lines AND a nine-category summary footing to a printed grand total, which is what let both of those years be read and checked. FY2016 prints neither, so the page cannot be footed, the receipts cannot be classified into the Town's own categories, and what the Town took in during FY2016 is not stated in this report. — closes: the Treasurer's FY2016 cash receipts report as the accounting system produces it, the same report whose later editions the FY2020 and FY2021 annual reports print in full.

rows.what: Which capital project is the unnamed $25,000.00 on the FY2016 capital projects schedule?
rows.why: THE PAGE PRINTS A RULED ROW WITH A FIGURE AND NO NAME. On `CAPITAL PROJECT FUNDS FY 2016`, PDF page 36 of the FY2016 annual town report, the row between the column header and `08/02 ATM Development of Cemeteries` carries $25,000.00 in APPROPRIATED FORWARD and nothing else -- no purpose, no article reference, no `fwd` flag, no expended figure, no balance. IT IS NOT A READING ERROR AND IT IS NOT IGNORABLE. All three columns of the page tie to the printed Grand Total to the cent only when that $25,000.00 is counted, so the figure is part of the schedule. And the Cemeteries row immediately below it does not close as printed -- $1,019.01 less $35,229.38 is ($34,210.37) against a printed balance of ($9,210.37), short by exactly $25,000.00. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: that the $25,000.00 belongs to the Cemeteries project. A label that failed to print, a second article against the same project, and a separate project whose text was lost all fit the same evidence, and nothing in the report tests between them. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2016 capital project fund detail by article, which names the article every capital appropriation sits under.

rows.what: What were Lunenburg’s fiscal 2011 class valuations, where the town’s own two printings disagree by $7,295,100?
rows.why: The FY2011 annual town report prints the same quantity twice on one page (PDF p12, printed folio 9) and the two do not reconcile. `Fiscal 2011 Assessments and Revenues by Major Property Class` puts Commercial at 64,514,700 and foots its tax levy to the printed 18,006,811.48 to the cent; the `Fiscal Year 2011 Abstract of Assessments` below it puts `300 - 393 Commercial` at 56,208,300 and `600 - 821 Chapter 61, 61A, 61B` at 1,011,300, so its twelve classes sum to 1,106,987,789 against its own printed TOTALS of 1,114,282,889. The residual is 7,295,100 and it sits entirely in the commercial class: the abstract’s eight residential lines sum to 1,000,004,500, which is the first table’s Residential valuation to the dollar, and its account count ties exactly at 5,185, so no row is missing from the reading. Both cells were re-read off the page’s own 400 dpi bitmap at 6x. Which printing is wrong is not established, and the report itself settles nothing — the first table’s own TOTALS cell is misprinted `1,114,2828,889`, ten digits. — closes: the Assessors’ certified fiscal 2011 Tax Recapitulation (DOR Form LA-4/LA-5) for Lunenburg, which states valuation by class as the Department of Revenue certified it and is the only document that outranks both printings.

rows.what: Which of the FY2011 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?
rows.why: Page 58 of the FY2011 annual town report prints 90 receipt lines under ten block headings and then a nine-category `SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS` footed to a GRAND TOTAL of $27,388,537.87. The summary ties to the cent, and every detail figure on the page is now transcribed, but the page never says which detail line belongs to which category and the headings are not the categories — ten blocks against nine categories, one block unheaded, and `FEES` naming both a block and a category without the two agreeing. Five categories can be reproduced exactly (LICENSES AND PERMITS, STATE REVENUE, SPECIAL ASSESSMENTS, INVESTMENT INCOME, TRANSFER FROM OTHER FUNDS); four cannot. TAXES & EXCISES comes out $23,947.19 OVER its printed total, FINES & FORFEITS $2,025.00 SHORT, and FEES ($502,520.65) and NON RECURRING REVENUE ($71,325.29) cannot be reconstructed by any grouping the page states. So the town’s own revenue mix for FY2011 — how much is tax, how much is fee, how much is one-off — cannot be read off the document that reports it. This is the same limit already registered for FY2016, FY2020 and FY2021 and it recurs because the format does. — closes: the Treasurer’s or Accountant’s FY2011 receipts detail as the accounting system prints it, with each receipt account carrying its revenue classification (a MUNIS revenue report by account), which is the only document that states the mapping rather than assuming it.

rows.what: What are the $25,276.56 of fines and $3,110.00 of fees that FY2012 receipts counts but does not name?
rows.why: The FY2012 annual town report, PDF p58 (`FY 2012 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2012`), prints 91 detail lines and a nine-category SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS. The nine categories foot to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $28,471,842.32 exactly; the 91 lines sum to $28,443,455.76, short by $28,386.56. Seven of the nine categories are reproduced to the cent by a partition of those lines, which puts the whole shortfall in two: FINES & FORFEITS, where the page prints only PARKING FINES $2,120.25 and DOG FINES $2,550.00 against a category total of $29,946.81, and FEES, short by $3,110.00. The page was swept end to end and prints no further row, so this is the document omitting detail rather than our reading missing it. Court fines are the obvious candidate for the larger figure and nothing in the report says so. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2012 general ledger revenue detail (MUNIS), which lists every receipt account by code rather than by the summary categories this page prints.

rows.what: Which figure is wrong in the FY2013 Omnibus Budget: the eleven section totals, or the $600 larger Total Omnibus?
rows.why: The budget Town Meeting voted under Article 8 is printed in the FY2012 annual town report, PDF pp.81-82. Every one of its eleven sections foots to its own printed subtotal exactly, and those eleven subtotals sum to $27,488,841.00 against a printed `Total Omnibus` of $27,489,441.00 — six hundred dollars more. Both figures were re-read upright at full scale off the page's own 518 dpi bitmap, so this is the document disagreeing with itself and not a misreading. The $600 could be a line the page does not print, a section total understated, or the grand total overstated, and nothing on those two pages distinguishes them. — closes: the Town Clerk's certified copy of the Article 8 motion and the FY2013 budget handouts it refers to (`Refer to Handouts on pages 27 – 30`), which the annual report does not reproduce.

rows.what: What the $600.00 is between the FY2013 receipts page's own detail and its own GRAND TOTAL
rows.why: PDF page 63 of the FY2013 annual town report prints `FY 2013 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2013`: 91 detail lines in three label/amount column-pairs, and beside them a nine-line SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS footing to a printed GRAND TOTAL of $29,744,547.31. The nine summary categories sum to that GRAND TOTAL EXACTLY. The 91 detail lines sum to $29,743,947.31 -- $600.00 less. The reading is not the problem: the page has no text layer and was read off its own 400 dpi bitmap twice, and three of its printed detail blocks foot to their matching summary line to the cent (LICENSES/PERMITS to 174,193.45, STATE REVENUE to 7,010,803.56, FINES & FORFEITS to 27,405.00), which bounds the difference away from 29 of the 91 lines and leaves it inside the fees and departmental revenue lines. The page never states that the detail is exhaustive of the summary, so this is NOT recorded as the town's arithmetic failing -- it may be one receipt listed only in the summary, a line printed $600 low, or two different universes. Nothing on the page distinguishes them. sources/data/page-reads/fy2013-p63-*.csv. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2013 year-end revenue report out of the accounting system (the MUNIS revenue ledger for fiscal 2013, which this project already holds for FY2026 as sources/munis-ledgers/revenue/), which lists receipts by account and foots itself.

rows.what: Does FY2024's debt service include the Mass Water Pool 9 balloon payment, or not?
rows.why: The FY2013 annual town report's debt repayment schedule (PDF pages 81-82) prints, in its 2024 column, GRAND TOTAL PRINCIPAL 846,635 and GRAND TOTAL INTEREST 120,310 -- 966,945 -- against a printed TOTAL DEBT of 548,241. The document is out by 418,704 in that one column, and by the same 418,704 in its own TOTAL column (24,298,664 + 7,307,840 = 31,606,504 against a printed 31,187,800). Every other year of the 34 closes exactly. The figures were read off the page's own 400 dpi bitmap twice. 418,704 is also the principal the FY2014 annual report prints for `MASS WATER POOL 9*` in the FY2024 column -- the only row in that report's 156-row schedule with a principal and NO interest and NO total beside it (sources/data/page-reads/fy2014-p40-debt-schedule.csv). So the discrepancy is located on one borrowing, and it is still not known whether the town excludes that payment from debt service on purpose because the Trust subsidises it, or whether one of the two printed figures is simply wrong. The difference matters: it is 76% of what the town otherwise shows itself owing in FY2024. The per-issue rows of the FY2013 schedule are NOT read -- that limit is already registered as “What does each individual debt issue cost the town in a given year” and is not refiled here. — closes: the Treasurer's debt service schedule for the Mass Water Pollution Abatement Trust loan numbered 9, showing the FY2024 payment and any Trust subsidy against it.

rows.what: What did Lunenburg owe, by borrowing and by fiscal year, from FY2020 to FY2035?
rows.why: FY2019 PDF pages 49-52 print the whole forward debt repayment schedule -- about seventeen named borrowings against sixteen fiscal-year columns, each printed as PRINCIPAL / INTEREST / ADMIN FEE under a TOTAL row, on the order of 800 cells. It is fully self-proving (PRINCIPAL + INTEREST + ADMIN FEE = TOTAL, per issue per year, roughly 270 independent assertions). None of it has been read: `debt-repayment-detail-refused.csv` records 3 issue rows on p50 and 5 on p52 and no closing block, because the column header band at the top of each page sits inside the top 22.7% that the clipped render discarded. So the town's own forward debt service for sixteen years is published and unread. - closes: nothing from the Town is needed. The pages are legible at 150 dpi; this closes by reading them, after the document is re-OCR'd with the current renderer so the header band is visible. RESOLVED 2 October 2026: read in full, and the sizing in this row was wrong in every figure — it is FIFTEEN borrowings not seventeen, TWENTY-EIGHT fiscal years plus a TOTAL column not sixteen, 879 printed figures not ~800, and 213 issue-year identities not ~270. Measured off the pages. 198 of 213 close exactly and the 15 that miss by $1 are every one of them a Mass Water Pool trust line, which is displayed-dollar rounding and not a misread: bond principal, the column with no cents beneath it, ties exactly for 13 of 15 issues and the fifteen printed issue principals sum to $46,568,549 at ZERO tolerance.

rows.what: What did each of the ~130 individual receipt lines on the FY2019 receipts page bring in?
rows.why: PDF page 30 of the FY2019 annual town report (printed folio 28), `FY 2019 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2019`, prints about 130 named receipt lines in three label/amount column pairs, and separately a nine-category `SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS` with a GRAND TOTAL. The SUMMARY is now read and closes to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $40,734,004.07 to the cent (`sources/data/page-reads/fy2019-p30-receipts.csv`). THE DETAIL IS NOT READ. The page is a ~150 dpi photograph with no text layer, and recognition finds only about 75 of the ~130 printed money figures, so the second identity the page states about itself -- that the detail lines also sum to the GRAND TOTAL -- is untested. Until it is, FY2019 has category subtotals and no line-level receipts, so questions like what the town took in from building permits or from ambulance billing cannot be answered for that year from this page. - closes: nothing from the Town is needed and no better scan is required; the page is legible. This closes by transcribing the three column pairs and footing them to the nine category subtotals already proven, which is about 130 figures against ten independent assertions.

rows.what: Which figure did the 2019 Annual Town Meeting vote for Central Purchasing, where the printed FY 2020 Omnibus Budget prints two that are a factor of ten apart?
rows.why: The budget is printed on pages 161-164 of the FY2019 annual town report (printed pages 159-162) and the document contradicts itself in two places. p162 prints `38 Central Purchasing $ 603,030.00` and, three rows beneath it, `Total Central Purchasing $ 60,303.00` -- $542,727.00 apart. And p162 prints four Fire lines (1,093,374.24 + 20,000.00 + 15,000.00 + 10,000.00 = 1,138,374.24) above `Subtotal Fire Dept. $1,138,434.24`, $60.00 more than its own lines. Sixteen of the eighteen printed group totals foot their own line items to the cent and the twelve section totals sum to the printed `Total Omnibus $38,058,164.30` exactly, so this is the town's arithmetic and not our reading: both pairs were read at 400 dpi off the page's own bitmap. The town's grand total is footed on $60,303.00 and on $1,138,434.24, so the printed Total Omnibus cannot distinguish a misprinted line from a misprinted subtotal. A resident cannot tell from the published report what Central Purchasing was authorised to spend in FY2020, and the two readings differ by more than half a million dollars. -- closes: the Town Clerk's certified record of the vote on the FY2020 omnibus budget article at the 2019 Annual Town Meeting, with the schedule attached to the motion as moved.

rows.what: Whether a board discussed a thing at a meeting it noticed but left no minutes and no recording of
rows.why: 1,754 of the 6,990 meetings in sources/data/meeting-register.csv (25%) have a posted AGENDA and neither minutes nor a recording, so the only surviving record is that the meeting was noticed and what it meant to take up. 235 of them are since 1 July 2024. It is worst where a body is small: School Advisory Councils & Committees 229 of 268 (85%), Capital Planning 63 of 182 (35%), Board of Health 101 of 297 (34%). WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not evidence that nothing was discussed, and a search that returns nothing for one of these dates has not searched the meeting -- it has searched an agenda. The practical cost is the inverse question. Parks Commission can be shown DISCUSSING its budget (44 of 192 meeting dates carry the word, and `Budget / Finance Review` is a named agenda item from 22 July 2026), and cannot be shown NOT to have, because 40 of its 193 meetings left no account at all -- including 30 September 2026, whose agenda item was `Budget Check-in`. This is distinct from the register's own limit, that a meeting with no agenda either is indistinguishable from one never held: here the town has published a notice, so the meeting is established and only its content is missing. — closes: the minutes themselves. G.L. c.30A §22 requires a public body to create and maintain accurate minutes of every meeting and to make them available on request, so for each of these dates the document is owed whether or not it was ever posted to the AgendaCenter. Requested by board and date.

rows.what: Why the school department's FY2024 actual spending differs between its period 13 ledger and the general fund history, on 12 of 265 lines
rows.why: Measured 5 October 2026 from the Finance Committee files: the period 13 report (`glytdbud`, generated 7 August 2024) and the FY2010-FY2025 general fund history agree to the cent on 253 of 265 school general-fund lines; 12 differ, by a net 243,636.29, the history higher -- led by a paraprofessional line and a clerical salary line, with some lines moving the other way. Entries posted to FY2024 after 7 August 2024 would produce this pattern; nothing here tests that. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2024 journal entries posted after 7 August 2024 for fund 0100, department 300.

rows.what: What a level-service budget for each town department would have cost, year by year
rows.why: The general fund history the Finance Committee supplied holds each department’s original budget, transfers, revised budget and actual spending, FY2010–FY2025, and no request: nothing in it says what a department asked for or what keeping its service level would have cost. The schools present a level-service budget, and its difference from the appropriation is what is reported as the school deficit. For the town’s departments no equivalent figure is in this archive for any year before FY2027 — the year the Town Manager asked department heads for level-service budgets (Finance Committee minutes, 12 February 2026) and the override questions covered town and school alike — so whether they would have shown a gap in earlier years cannot be measured, and the difference between the two sides may be one of process rather than of cost. — closes: each town department’s budget request as submitted to the Town Manager, with the Town Manager’s recommendation beside it, for each fiscal year, held by the Town Manager’s office.

rows.what: What the money was that reached departments’ revised budgets outside any recorded transfer
rows.why: In the general fund history the revised budget differs from original plus transfers in and out on about one account-year in twenty, almost always upward, in every year FY2010–FY2025, and the workbook’s own Grand Total shows the same gap. By dollars, most of it is no larger than what the same account left unspent the year before, which is what a carried-forward encumbrance would look like; the rest fits a supplemental appropriation at a special Town Meeting. Neither is confirmed, and the difference matters: a carry-forward is last year’s money, a supplemental appropriation is new money. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the MUNIS budget amendment detail for each fiscal year, or the Town Accountant’s appropriations schedule with its APPROPRIATED FORWARD column, which the annual report printed through FY2023.

rows.what: Whether a town department’s budget growth is more service or a cost moved into it from another budget
rows.why: Several town departments’ starting budgets grew in single steps — general highway maintenance, facilities and grounds, public buildings and recycling each have one year in which the starting budget rose by more than a third — and a step that size fits a service being taken on, or a cost moved in from another line or fund, as well as it fits the same service costing more. The ledger records dollars by account and nothing about why an account moved, so a growth rate measured across such a step is not a trend. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the Town Manager’s budget message, or the Finance Committee’s report to Town Meeting, for each year in which a department’s starting budget stepped.

rows.what: Why the general fund’s starting budget grew more slowly than the levy limit, FY2010 to FY2025
rows.why: Measured from the general fund history against the Division of Local Services’ certified levy limits, the whole starting budget grew more slowly each year, on average, than the levy limit did — even with the FY2025 override taken back out of the limit. Three readings fit: the rest of the revenue (state aid, local receipts, free cash) grew more slowly than the levy; the town levied below its limit; or money raised under the limit went outside the general fund operating budget, to capital articles or enterprise subsidies. They imply different things about how much room the levy has left. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the Tax Rate Recapitulation for each fiscal year, which states the levy actually raised, the excess levy capacity and every other source the budget was balanced with.

rows.what: Where did the $122,502.44 that moved out of the FY2025 school department mid-year go, and what posted to department 300 after the School Committee's 17 September 2025 surplus statement?
rows.why: The closed MUNIS ledger (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv, FY2025 period 13, department 300) carries transfers_adjustments as a net figure per account, with no counterparty -- so a line moved in cannot be matched to the line it moved out of. And the ledger's own $627,116.86 available at the close exceeds the $603,885.97 the district reported that day by $23,230.89, with no single account or pair of accounts equal to the gap, which is consistent with activity posted after 17 September 2025 but not established by anything held here. — closes: the FY2025 transfer schedule for department 300 with counterparties and authority, and the journal entries posted to department 300 after 17 September 2025.

rows.what: How many children enter or leave an out-of-district placement during a school year, and when?
rows.why: Only two snapshots are published, months apart and taken by different bodies: DESE's count of students with disabilities placed out of district in October, and the town's count of placements on 1 March in the Special Services report of each annual town report. Their difference is a NET change -- an arrival and a departure between the two dates cancel, and a child placed and returned between them is in neither -- and some of it may be the two bodies counting differently. DESE's caseload-movement file (8aww-sugs) counts children entering and leaving special education SERVICES, not placements. The district has said at public meetings that children have moved in already needing a placement and that a child entering after 1 April is the sending district's cost; neither is a count. A mid-year reserve for tuition is sized by exactly this number, which is why /analysis/special-education-costs cannot size one from children and sizes it from the ledger instead. — closes: the district's out-of-district placement log, one row per placement with its start date, end date and setting (collaborative, day or residential) and no names, from the Director of Student Services by records request.

rows.what: What does one out-of-district placement cost Lunenburg in a year?
rows.why: DESE publishes what the district spent on tuition to private schools and collaboratives (functions 9300 and 9400), by fund, and the town publishes how many children were placed on 1 March. Nothing in this archive prices a single placement. /analysis/special-education-costs divides the first by the second and labels the result our estimate; /what-special-education-costs refuses to, and both are right about what the quotient is not: it mixes residential, day and collaborative places, it counts a child placed for part of a year as either a whole year or nothing depending on one day, and transportation is in a different line. A reserve for an unplanned placement needs the price of one, and the only figure available is that estimate. — closes: the accounts-payable detail behind general fund and fund 2640 accounts in functions 9300 and 9400 -- vendor, invoice period and amount, no student names -- from the Town Accountant, or the district's tuition rate sheets for the year.

rows.what: Does segment 51 of a school account string mean special education?
rows.why: The town's account string is nine segments; the fourth is the DESE function code. The fifth is 51 on every general fund school account whose own description names special education, except special education transportation, and /analysis/special-education-costs classifies in-district special education by it -- less two accounts the district's own budget book labels as English learner costs, which shows the segment is not purely special education. The meaning of the segment is read from the account names, not from a published chart of accounts, so the in-district total rests on our reading. — closes: the Town's MUNIS chart of accounts, with the definition of each segment and its values, from the Town Accountant.

rows.what: How much the Special Education Reserve Fund holds, and what the law lets it do
rows.why: Special Town Meeting on 18 November 2025 accepted Mass. General Laws chapter 40 section 13E and established a Special Education Reserve Fund for unanticipated or unbudgeted special education, out-of-district tuition and transportation costs (FY2025 annual town report). The Town Manager told the Select Board on 7 October 2025 that spending from it needs a majority of both the School Committee and the Select Board and that its balance may not exceed 2% of annual net school spending. The statute itself is not in this archive, so the cap and the vote are as described at a meeting; and no balance, deposit or withdrawal is in any ledger held here. The School Committee's agenda for 7 October 2026 carries an item to vote an amount to fund it. — closes: the text of chapter 40 section 13E (malegislature.gov, public); and the Treasurer's balance of the fund with every vote to fund or spend it, from the Town Accountant.

rows.what: How much of the $236,766.94 still encumbered in the FY2026 school general fund at period 13 will be paid, how much released to the surplus, and how much carried into FY2027?
rows.why: The FY2026 period-13 MUNIS report for department 300 (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv), run on 6 October 2026, shows $482,118.07 unspent and $236,766.94 still encumbered across 27 accounts -- the largest electricity ($62,362.13) and collaborative tuitions ($58,708.07). Between the period-12 run of 1 September 2026 and that run, spending did not move in any account and one encumbrance of $16.95 was released, so the FY26 school surplus is still anywhere from $482,118.07 to $718,885.01. The FY2025 report run the same day shows nothing encumbered. A ledger shows a commitment, not whether it will be paid, cancelled or carried forward, and which of those happens decides the surplus. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus. — closes: the FY2026 period-13 report for department 300 run again after the year-end close, and the Town Accountant's list of FY2026 encumbrances carried forward into FY2027, by account.

rows.what: What was the School Committee told under "FY26 Year End Budget review" on 2 and 9 September 2026?
rows.why: Both agendas carry the item (Old Business, 5 minutes). The archive's catalogue of the Town's AgendaCenter lists no minutes for either meeting, so the only written statement on the FY26 school year-end held here is the 29 July 2026 minutes, in which the business manager was "confident the remaining amount would be well below" the approximately $600,000 returned in FY25. The machine captions of the recordings can locate a moment but are not a record. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus. — closes: the approved School Committee minutes of 2 and 9 September 2026, and any year-end budget document presented under that item.

rows.what: What does each individual debt issue cost the town in a given year, and which of them fall off when?
rows.why: FY2022 NO LONGER BELONGS TO THIS GAP: its schedule was read by issue on 29 September 2026 -- 14 borrowings against 25 fiscal years, 184 issue-years, each closing on its own printed TOTAL row and reconciling to the GRAND TOTAL block on pages 46 and 48. rows.what: How many financial pages do the annual town reports actually contain?
rows.why: The page tracker's universe is built from what RECOGNITION found: a page is listed only if fifteen money figures were recognised on it. FY2024 page 189 prints ninety-six wages and recognition found ZERO, so it was not unfinished, it was ABSENT -- and five of the eight pages of that wage run were. FY2024 was reported as 22 financial pages and is at least 28. A page a person has now read is added to the map, so the eight are on it; nothing finds the pages nobody has looked at yet, and the same failure is unmeasured in the other fifteen reports. A screen for candidates -- many boxes, almost no recognised money -- returns about 1,800 pages archive-wide, but it catches every page of ordinary prose too and is a finding aid rather than a count. — closes: nothing from the Town. Every page is already held; what is missing is somebody looking at the ones recognition could not read.

rows.what: Which of the town's two FY2023 statements of what the special revenue and enterprise funds held is right?
rows.why: The FY2023 combined balance sheet gives special revenue fund equity as 6,131,303.68 and enterprise fund equity as 3,812,502.24, together 9,943,805.92. The special revenue schedule in the SAME annual report prints a grand total carried forward of 10,031,099.78. They are 87,293.86 apart. The comparison ties to the cent in FY2011, FY2013, FY2019 and FY2022, and the balance sheet's own arithmetic is complete -- every column foots to its own printed totals and liabilities plus equity equals assets -- so this is two published tables disagreeing and not a reading error. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2023 trial balance, which would say which of the two the books support.

rows.what: What did the town receive in FY2023, receipt line by receipt line?
rows.why: The FY2023 receipts page -- annual report page 25 -- cannot be read. It is a photograph embedded at 93 dpi, and it packs about 150 line items across three column-pairs of a landscape page, so the digits are below the resolution of the stored image: `588` and `568`, `405` and `465`, `009` and `000` are not distinguishable at any magnification, because the detail is not in the file to magnify. Reading the SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block gives a total $20 from the printed GRAND TOTAL of $45,549,438.56, consistent with exactly one misread digit, and choosing the digit that makes it close would be fitting the answer to the check. For contrast the same report stores page 50 at 183 dpi and page 53 at 156 dpi, and both are legible. RE-CHECKED 1 October 2026 off the page's own embedded bitmap rather than off the recognition cache, with the grid measured by projection and the amount columns rendered at 20x: the labels are legible and the figures are not, so what the town received money FOR in FY2023 is readable and how much is not. **And a better scan is not a remedy that exists.** Of the two publisher addresses on record, DocumentCenter/View/4131 now returns HTTP 404 and ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/160 returns 18,274,143 bytes -- byte-for-byte the copy this archive already holds. — closes: the Treasurer's own FY2023 receipts file, or a MUNIS revenue report for FY2023; this archive holds neither, and no MUNIS revenue export for any year.

rows.what: Why does DESE's FY2024 figure for out-of-district tuition paid from funds other than the general fund exceed what the circuit breaker account paid by exactly the FY2024 circuit breaker payment?
rows.why: DESE's End of Year Financial Report reports FY2024 tuition (functions 9300 and 9400) paid from funds other than the general fund. The town's year-end report for the school special funds shows what the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) paid in tuition that year. The remainder between the two is, to the dollar, the circuit breaker payment DESE's reimbursement file lists for FY2024; in FY2023 and FY2025 the remainder is small. The figures are computed, not typed, in the report's payload under circuit_breaker.unexplained. It may be a coincidence, a second fund, or the receipt reported as an expenditure; nothing in this archive distinguishes them, so /analysis/special-education-costs shows the figure as 'other funds' and says it cannot explain it. Computed in scripts/build_sped_costs.py, which refuses to print the sentence if the equality stops holding. — closes: the district's FY2024 End of Year Financial Report as submitted to DESE (Schedule 1 by fund), or the school special funds year-end report for any fund other than 2640 that paid tuition in FY2024.

rows.what: Was the FY2026 school surplus thrift — did discretionary spending slow late in the year?
rows.why: A speaker at the School Committee on 7 October 2026 said, per our machine captions, "We were thrifty"; no posted minutes record a decision to hold FY2026 spending. The period-13 ledger shows where money was left (by our category table, 59% of it in supplies, upkeep and equipment) but only as year-end totals, so restraint, a postponed project and a line budgeted high look identical. — closes: the school general-fund journal (MUNIS GL detail) for department 300 by month, FY2023 to FY2026, so discretionary spending in the last quarter can be set against prior years.

rows.what: Which school counselor, social-worker and psychologist posts were vacant or on leave in FY2026, and for how long?
rows.why: The FY2026 period-13 ledger leaves these salary lines well under budget — one psychologist account spent nothing of its budget — and no posted minutes explain it. A dollar is not a post (rule 11): vacancy, leave, a lower hiring step and contracted cover all produce the same row. — closes: the district’s position-control roster by month for functions 2710 and 2800, each budgeted post with who held it and from when.

rows.what: Why FY2026 private special-education tuition came in far under budget while collaborative tuition ran far over
rows.why: In the FY2026 period-13 ledger the general fund’s private-tuition line (9300) ended well under budget and its collaborative-tuition line (9400) well over, netting to a small surplus; the circuit breaker fund (2640) paid collaborative tuition that year and no private tuition, the reverse of FY2025. Fewer private placements, placements moved to collaboratives, and the line a payment was charged to all fit the same rows. — closes: the FY2026 out-of-district placement list by setting, with start dates and each tuition invoice and the fund it was paid from.

rows.what: What the town’s own special revenue funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026
rows.why: The annual town reports print every special revenue fund's balance at 30 June, and this project has read and proved FY2011 to FY2023 -- forward, receipts, disbursements and carried, every row and every printed GRAND TOTAL tying (special-revenue-read.csv). FY2024 and FY2025 print a DIFFERENT table, a balance detail with no receipts or disbursements, no row identity and no stable fund key: it is printed and has not yet been read into a dataset, which is our gap rather than the town's. FY2026's annual report is not yet published. The school side of 'is anyone sitting on money' runs to 30 June 2026 through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers; the town side stops at 30 June 2023, so whether the town's own funds kept growing cannot be said. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report (or trial balance) at period 13 for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 covering the town's special revenue funds -- the same system that produced the school delivery of 6 October 2026, pointed at the town's funds.

rows.what: What the school grant funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026
rows.why: Fourteen school funds -- circuit breaker, school choice, lunch, eight fee-funded revolving funds and three gift funds -- are carried from the annual report's 30 June 2023 balance through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers, and the result ties to the cent to the Town's March 2026 special revenue report for every one. The grant funds cannot be carried that way: the annual report names a grant by programme and year, MUNIS numbers it, and nothing published maps one to the other; and a reimbursement grant spends before it is paid, so one year's revenue less expense is not a change in what it holds. So the school total after 2023 covers the fourteen and not the grants. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report at period 13 for the school grant funds (26xx-29xx), FY2024 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance.

rows.what: Why local receipts come in above the town’s own estimate
rows.why: The state's free cash proof shows receipts above the town's estimate (its line CL#6) as one of the largest components of Lunenburg's free cash in every one of the five years it covers, and above a million dollars in four of them. On 28 May 2026 a Finance Committee member told the committee the town had not collected less than four million dollars in local receipts in ten years, against a current estimate of 3.535 million. Three readings fit the same line: an estimate set low on purpose as a buffer; receipts that grew faster than any forecast could know; or one-time receipts that should not be estimated at all. They imply different things about how much of each year's free cash is predictable, and so about how much the budget could count on. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: the town's local receipts estimate against actual collections, by category, for each year -- the local receipts page of each year's Tax Rate Recapitulation beside DLS Schedule A.

rows.what: How much of the special education circuit breaker account's balance is already committed to the next year's tuition?
rows.why: The account (fund 2640) pays out-of-district tuition every year, overrun or not, and its 30 June balance is computed on /analysis/special-education-costs and /analysis/sitting-on-money. Whether that balance is free to meet a mid-year surprise, or is already planned against next year's placements, is not published: the year-end ledgers show what was spent, not what was intended, and in one year the account carried a tuition budget while in the others it carried none. So a resident cannot tell how much of the balance is a cushion beside the new special education reserve. — closes: the district's circuit breaker spending plan for the year, or the budget narrative for the out-of-district tuition line stating how much it assumes the account will pay.

rows.what: Which school special revenue funds the period-13 special funds report leaves out
rows.why: The FY2023 annual town report's special revenue schedule prints $3,667,636 received and $4,333,280 spent across every school special revenue fund; the MUNIS period-13 special funds report for the same year, delivered 6 October 2026, carries $2,440,883 and $2,962,716. The difference is funds that report does not carry -- among them, the annual report's FY22 ESSER II #115, FY22 ARP Idea #252 and FY22 Idea ARP #264 rows have no fund of that name or number in the MUNIS report. And the FY2026 report books $59,333 of grant revenue against $557,427 of grant spending. A reimbursement booked after the close, a grant receipt held in a fund outside the report, and both together all fit; the report cannot separate them, so whether the schools spend the grant money that comes in can be said only for the funds it carries. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the MUNIS period-13 revenue and expense report for EVERY school special revenue fund, FY2023 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance (or the trial balance for funds 2xxx at each close).

rows.what: What a fee-funded school programme costs that is not booked to its own fund
rows.why: A revolving fund that takes in more than it spends covers the costs BOOKED TO IT, and nothing more (rule 11). The ledger can test whether the general fund also carries a programme's costs only where both book to the same programme-specific DESE function code, and among the schools' fee and lunch funds that is true of athletics alone (function 3510, where the general fund booked most of the four years' athletics spending). Extended day, after-school activities, facilities rental and adult education book their spending to function codes that name no programme -- 2000, 4000, 5200 -- so whether the general fund pays any of their custodians, utilities, administration or benefits cannot be shown either way. 'Pays its own way' therefore cannot be stated for any of them beyond their own books. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the district's indirect-cost allocation for each revolving programme, or a cost study listing the general fund accounts that carry part of each programme's cost.

rows.what: What was paid from the school budget lines that spent against a $0 budget, FY2023–FY2026
rows.why: The closed MUNIS ledger (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv, report gf-school, period 13) gives one spent figure per account per year and nothing else: not the payee, not the warrant, not whether it was salary for a person or a coding correction. /analysis/spent-with-no-budget lists every general fund line that spent against a $0 voted budget; for every one of them, what the money bought is unknown. — closes: a MUNIS general ledger detail (journal) export for department 300, FY2023–FY2026, for those accounts, with the warrant or payroll reference on each entry.

rows.what: Whether the FY2026 spending on the kindergarten aide lines paid for aides in kindergarten classrooms
rows.why: The ledger books FY2026 spending to two accounts titled kindergarten aides and kindergarten paraprofessionals (orgs S2032121 and S2032131), both voted at $0; a Finance Committee minute of 12 January 2026 records the School Committee chair saying kindergarten classrooms had no aides. An account title is not a person in a room: staff coded to the line while assigned elsewhere, a reclassification, or posts moved between lines all print the same ledger, and nothing published joins the account to a building. — closes: the FY2026 payroll distribution for the two accounts, naming position and building (names may be redacted).
